This is the complete source note at compilation time. Its original experiment date, protocol, limitations and historical status apply; later corrections in the overview and subsequent audit notes take precedence. Heading levels, line endings, outer document spacing and source-relative Markdown links are normalized here; code and mathematical expressions are preserved.

### Exact nonlinear PDE identities

Sparse exponential polynomials provide an exact representation that supports
pointwise multiplication as well as differentiation. Their rational quotients
can represent nonconstant Cole–Hopf fields and check coupled nonlinear PDEs by
coefficient arithmetic. This extends the kinds of identities represented in the
library; it does not supply a general nonlinear PDE solver or a new
linearization theorem.

The [profile quotient](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias/docs/profile-pde.md) represents differential operators acting
on a profile family. It is not an algebra of pointwise products of those
profiles. Here the input is a **concrete function**, represented explicitly as

\[
P(x)=\sum_{(\lambda,\alpha)}c_{\lambda,\alpha}
x^\alpha e^{\lambda\cdot x},
\qquad c_{\lambda,\alpha}\in\mathbb Q,
\quad \lambda\in\mathbb Q^d,
\quad \alpha\in\mathbb N^d.
\]

The sum is finite. Canonicalization combines equal frequency/multi-index pairs
and removes zero coefficients. Coefficients and frequencies use exact rational
arithmetic; no small coefficient is discarded by a numerical tolerance.

#### Closure and exact coefficient comparison

Products add frequencies and polynomial powers:

\[
(x^\alpha e^{\lambda\cdot x})(x^\beta e^{\mu\cdot x})
=x^{\alpha+\beta}e^{(\lambda+\mu)\cdot x}.
\]

Differentiation has two contributions:

\[
\partial_i(x^\alpha e^{\lambda\cdot x})
=\alpha_i x^{\alpha-e_i}e^{\lambda\cdot x}
+\lambda_i x^\alpha e^{\lambda\cdot x}.
\]

The first term is omitted when \(\alpha_i=0\). These identities prove closure
under addition, multiplication and all finite partial derivatives.

Coefficient comparison is also necessary for an identity on a nonempty open
set. Group a putative zero as \(\sum_\lambda P_\lambda(x)e^{\lambda\cdot x}\).
Choose a direction \(v\) so that all \(\lambda\cdot v\) are distinct. For a fixed
\(\lambda\), apply

\[
\prod_{\mu\ne\lambda}
(D_v-\mu\cdot v)^{\deg P_\mu+1}.
\]

Every other exponential mode vanishes. On the remaining polynomial this acts
as a product of operators \(D_v+(\lambda-\mu)\cdot v\), times the nonzero
exponential. Each factor is invertible on polynomials of bounded degree:
\(D_v\) is nilpotent there and the added constant is nonzero. The remaining
polynomial therefore vanishes if and only if \(P_\lambda=0\). Repeating for all
frequencies proves independence and the exact zero criterion.

This reasoning concerns functional identities on open sets. Vanishing only on
a sampled trajectory, a boundary plane or a finite point set does not imply
that every coefficient vanishes.

#### Rational fields retain their domains

For \(u=P/Q\), differentiation uses

\[
\partial_i u=\frac{(\partial_iP)Q-P(\partial_iQ)}{Q^2}.
\]

The numerator and denominator remain exponential polynomials. Addition,
multiplication and division are handled by the ordinary fraction identities.
An identically zero denominator or divisor is refused.

A rational field must retain all nonzero conditions introduced while building
it. Denote this finite set of guards by \(\Gamma\), and its regular domain by

\[
\Omega_\Gamma=\{x:g(x)\ne0\text{ for every }g\in\Gamma\}.
\]

Addition and multiplication inherit the guards of both operands.
Differentiation inherits the operand's guards. Reciprocation additionally
requires its numerator to be nonzero. Division inherits both operands' guards
and requires the divisor's numerator to be nonzero. Algebraic simplification
must preserve these conditions: \(P/P=1\) only where the original quotient was
defined. The same applies to multiplying a singular expression by zero or
taking its zeroth power.

Thus a zero numerator proves that the field is zero **on its regular domain**.
Cross multiplication proves equality on the common regular domain. Neither
claim establishes equality of partial-function domains or removes a pole. A
global PDE solution requires a separate nonvanishing argument for its guards.
For example, a nonempty sum of real exponentials with positive coefficients is
strictly positive everywhere. General signed denominators do not have this
automatic guarantee.

#### Cole–Hopf with several rates

For positive rational \(\nu,c_j\) and rational \(k_j\), let

\[
\tau(x,t)=\sum_j c_j e^{k_jx+\nu k_j^2t},
\qquad u=-2\nu\frac{\tau_x}{\tau}.
\]

Every mode solves \(\tau_t=\nu\tau_{xx}\), and positivity gives
\(\tau>0\) everywhere. Direct differentiation gives the stronger residual
identity

\[
u_t+uu_x-\nu u_{xx}
=-2\nu\,\partial_x\left(\frac{\tau_t-\nu\tau_{xx}}{\tau}\right).
\]

Consequently the field solves viscous Burgers' equation globally. The converse
does not require \(\tau_t-\nu\tau_{xx}=0\): the quotient on the right may depend
only on time. That distinction matters when inferring an equation for \(\tau\)
from one for \(u\).

A useful nonconstant example is
\(\tau=1+e^{x+t}+e^{2x+4t}\), with \(\nu=1\). This uses different temporal
rates and is not one travelling-wave profile. The construction is the classical
[Cole–Hopf transformation](https://doi.org/10.1090/qam/42889), and multiple-front
families have established [prior work](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amc.2007.02.003).

The example uses coordinate order \((t,x)\). All constants below are exact
integers; noninteger exact values can be supplied as `Fraction` objects.

```python
from omnibias.core.exp_polynomial import ExpPolynomial
from omnibias.core.rational_field import RationalField, discover_rational_relations

tau = (ExpPolynomial.constant(1, 2)
       + ExpPolynomial.exponential((1, 1))
       + ExpPolynomial.exponential((4, 2)))
u = RationalField(tau.differentiate(1).scale(-2), tau)
one = RationalField.from_polynomial(ExpPolynomial.constant(1, 2))
features = (u.differentiate(0), u*u.differentiate(1),
            u.differentiate(1, 2), u, one)
residual = features[0] + features[1] - features[2]
assert residual.is_zero()
assert all(g.known_global_sign() in (-1, 1)
           for g in residual.nonzero_conditions)

relations = discover_rational_relations((features,))
assert relations.rank == 4
assert len(relations.relations) == 1
a = relations.relations[0]
assert a[0] == a[1] == -a[2]
assert a[3] == a[4] == 0
```

The result contains every rational relation in this five-feature library. Its
one-dimensional nullspace identifies Burgers' equation up to nonzero scale.
The separate sign checks establish that these particular denominator guards
never vanish; `is_zero()` alone would not establish that fact.

The interval evaluator checks those same domain conditions before using an
algebraic zero:

```python
from omnibias.core.verified.exp_polynomial import evaluate_rational_field
from omnibias.core.verified.interval import Interval

enclosure = evaluate_rational_field(
    residual, (Interval(-1.0, 1.0), Interval(-2.0, 2.0)))
assert enclosure == Interval.point(0.0)
```

This exact zero with globally signed guards needs no transcendental backend.
Evaluating a nonzero exponential field requires the rigorous backend. General
guards must have interval enclosures excluding zero on the requested box;
failure is inconclusive and raises an exception. Finite-range overflow also
refuses evaluation. Exact identity checking and numerical enclosure remain
separate operations.

#### A coupled system in two spatial dimensions

The same construction gives a meaningful system test. For
\(x\in\mathbb R^d\), choose

\[
\tau(x,t)=\sum_j c_j e^{k_j\cdot x+\nu\lVert k_j\rVert^2t},
\qquad U=-2\nu\frac{\nabla\tau}{\tau}.
\]

It satisfies

\[
\partial_tU_i+\sum_j U_j\partial_jU_i-\nu\sum_j\partial_{jj}U_i=0,
\qquad
\partial_iU_j-\partial_jU_i=0.
\]

To verify the nonlinear equation, write \(q=\log\tau\). Then
\((U\cdot\nabla)U=2\nu^2\nabla\lVert\nabla q\rVert^2\), and the vector
residual becomes

\[
-2\nu\nabla\left(
q_t-\nu\Delta q-\nu\lVert\nabla q\rVert^2\right)
=-2\nu\nabla\left(\frac{\tau_t-\nu\Delta\tau}{\tau}\right)=0.
\]

The curl identity follows from commuting mixed derivatives. The irrotational
condition is substantive: this construction does not parameterize every
solution of the vector Burgers system. See [*The Hopf–Cole transformation,
topological solitons and multiple fusion solutions for the n-dimensional
Burgers system*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physleta.2015.09.033).

With coordinates \((t,x,y)\), a nonfactorizing test is

\[
\tau=1+e^{x+t}+e^{2y+4t}+2e^{x+y+2t},
\qquad (u,v)=-2(\tau_x,\tau_y)/\tau.
\]

Both cross-advection terms \(v u_y\) and \(u v_x\) are nonzero. Checking
\(u_t+u u_x+v u_y-u_{xx}-u_{yy}=0\), the corresponding equation for \(v\), and
\(u_y-v_x=0\) therefore exercises genuine coupling rather than two independent
scalar equations.

```python
def velocity(tau):
    return (RationalField(tau.differentiate(1).scale(-2), tau),
            RationalField(tau.differentiate(2).scale(-2), tau))

def features_for(field, u, v):
    one = RationalField.from_polynomial(
        ExpPolynomial.constant(1, 3, budget=field.budget))
    return (field.differentiate(0), u*field.differentiate(1),
            v*field.differentiate(2), field.differentiate(1, 2),
            field.differentiate(2, 2), u, v, one)

def combine(features, coefficients):
    first = features[0]
    result = RationalField.from_polynomial(
        ExpPolynomial.constant(0, first.dimension, budget=first.budget))
    for field, coefficient in zip(features, coefficients, strict=True):
        result = result + field.scale(coefficient)
    return result

tau = (ExpPolynomial.constant(1, 3)
       + ExpPolynomial.exponential((1, 1, 0))
       + ExpPolynomial.exponential((4, 0, 2))
       + ExpPolynomial.exponential((2, 1, 1), 2))
u, v = velocity(tau)
rows = (features_for(u, u, v), features_for(v, u, v))
relations = discover_rational_relations(rows)
assert relations.rank == 7
assert len(relations.relations) == 1
coefficients = relations.relations[0]
assert all(combine(row, coefficients).is_zero() for row in rows)
assert (u.differentiate(2) - v.differentiate(1)).is_zero()
assert not (v*u.differentiate(2)).is_zero()
assert not (u*v.differentiate(1)).is_zero()

# Validate the same discovered coefficients on different rates and directions.
held_out_tau = (ExpPolynomial.constant(1, 3)
                + ExpPolynomial.exponential((5, 2, -1), 2)
                + ExpPolynomial.exponential((2, -1, 1), 3)
                + ExpPolynomial.exponential((10, 1, 3)))
held_out_u, held_out_v = velocity(held_out_tau)
for field in (held_out_u, held_out_v):
    row = features_for(field, held_out_u, held_out_v)
    assert combine(row, coefficients).is_zero()
```

The eight columns are \((w_t,uw_x,vw_y,w_{xx},w_{yy},u,v,1)\), with one family
for \(w=u\) and one for \(w=v\). The shared relation supplies both PDE rows.
The held-out fields use different spatial directions and temporal rates, and
the coefficients are applied without refitting. Positivity of both heat
potentials makes the constructed velocities regular everywhere.

Polynomial parameters can also be represented as extra coordinates. For
\((t,x,y,a,b,c)\), use
\(\tau=1+a e^{x+t}+b e^{2y+4t}+c e^{x+y+2t}\), with zero exponential frequency
in the three parameter coordinates. Differentiating only physical axes
\(t,x,y\) holds the amplitudes fixed. The regression checks both nonlinear PDE
rows and recovers the same rank-seven relation by exact coefficient arithmetic
in all six coordinates. This proves the identities for every amplitude choice
on its regular domain, without sampling or fitting amplitudes. It does not
prove global regularity for arbitrary amplitudes: negative choices can make
\(\tau\) vanish, so its global-sign test is inconclusive over all of
\(\mathbb R^6\). Positive amplitudes give a separate global positivity proof.

A second regression represents the parameters as exponential biases instead:

\[
\tau=1+e^{t+x+a}+e^{4t+2y+b}+e^{2t+x+y+c}.
\]

Each term is constructed with `ExpPolynomial.exponential` in the six
coordinates. Both coupled PDE identities and the same discovered relation now
hold for **all real biases** \(a,b,c\), and `tau.known_global_sign()` returns
`1` over all of \(\mathbb R^6\). Physical differentiation still holds the
biases fixed. Changing a bias changes a positive modal amplitude while
preserving the heat-dispersion relation between spatial and temporal weights.

More generally, with scores
\(s_j=k_j\cdot x+\nu\lVert k_j\rVert^2t+b_j\), the classical Cole–Hopf
readout has the softmax form

\[
U=-2\nu\,\frac{\nabla\tau}{\tau}
=-2\nu\sum_j k_j\frac{e^{s_j}}{\sum_\ell e^{s_\ell}}.
\]

Include the constant term as \(k_0=0\), \(b_0=0\). This gives an exact nonlinear
PDE solution family with free biases and fixed dispersion weights. Its
guarantee uses exponential modes and the logarithmic derivative readout; other
activations or arbitrary network architectures need their own identity proof.

#### Exact discovery in a finite feature library

Suppose the proposed features are concrete rational fields
\(F_j=P_j/Q_j\), for example \(u_t\), \(uu_x\) and \(u_{xx}\). On their common
regular domain let \(D=\prod_jQ_j\). Then

\[
\sum_j a_jF_j=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\sum_j a_jP_j\prod_{k\ne j}Q_k=0.
\]

Expanding the right-hand side gives a finite rational matrix: a column for each
feature and a row for each frequency/multi-index pair. Its nullspace contains
exactly the rational coefficient relations in the supplied library. Stacking
the coefficient constraints for independently specified fields requires the
same relation to hold for every example. All denominator obligations remain
part of the result's interpretation. For nonlinear PDEs, linear combinations
of these solutions generally fail to be solutions; stacking imposes separate
identities on each supplied field.

`discover_rational_relations` returns `relations`, `rank`, `candidate_count`,
`constraint_count`, and the `nonzero_conditions` for each supplied family. Its
linear-algebra budget and the fields' exponential-polynomial budgets are
separate checks. Polynomial operations require matching dimensions and budget
values; resource refusal does not imply that an identity is false.

Cancellation does not remove domain obligations:

```python
denominator = (ExpPolynomial.exponential((1,))
               - ExpPolynomial.constant(1, 1))
singular = RationalField(ExpPolynomial.constant(1, 1), denominator)
zero = singular - singular
assert zero.is_zero()
assert zero.nonzero_conditions == singular.nonzero_conditions
assert (singular**0).nonzero_conditions == singular.nonzero_conditions
assert denominator.known_global_sign() is None
```

This zero expression still excludes \(x=0\), where its original denominator
vanishes. A `None` sign result is inconclusive; it does not itself prove a zero
exists. In this example, substitution at zero supplies that separate argument.

This is identification inside a finite library using complete structured
functions. It does not recover a unique physical law from arbitrary data. A
single field can satisfy additional identities, and an incomplete library can
miss the desired equation. Coefficients in a discovered PDE can be solved by
linear algebra because the features are fixed; simultaneously solving for
unknown solution parameters generally produces nonlinear algebraic equations.

#### Limits and relation to earlier methods

For prescribed periodic initial velocities, the
[Fourier heat construction](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias/docs/periodic-burgers.md) supplies a complementary
representation with rigorous exponential-series errors. It supports scalar
trigonometric data and coupled potential vector data, including spatial slope
sign changes excluded by positive sums of real exponential modes.

For the positive Cole–Hopf family, a prescribed velocity also defines a
[convex inverse problem](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias/docs/inverse-pde-map.md). Exact affine rank and an interval
root enclosure can certify the unique spatial input at a fixed time, and an
entropy witness gives a global objective bound. This is a separate inverse
query within the established solution family.

The representation initially uses rational coefficients and rational linear
exponents. It does not automatically convert every annihilator/profile pair,
admit arbitrary transcendental constants, or handle nested activations. A shift
of an exponential can introduce an irrational amplitude, so exact closure under
arbitrary bias translations must not be inferred from derivative closure.
The symbolic bias coordinates above keep these exponentials explicit; they do
not replace \(e^b\) with a rational constant.

Pointwise multiplication can grow the support, and a fixed finite profile space
cannot contain all such products. Indeed, a finite-dimensional unital algebra
of continuous real functions on a connected
domain contains only constants: the powers of any member \(f\) satisfy a
nonzero polynomial relation \(p(f)=0\), while a nonconstant continuous image
would contain an interval, contradicting the finite root set of \(p\). Exact
nonconstant multiplication therefore cannot be contained in a fixed finite
profile space. Term counts, arithmetic work and rational coefficient sizes need
explicit resource limits.

Rational exponential ansatz methods and coefficient matching have extensive
[prior art](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chaos.2006.03.020). Their use can produce
invalid or redundant claims without residual and domain checks; see
[*Be careful with the Exp-function method*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.4265).
The reusable capability here is exact, bounded identity checking with retained
domain conditions. It provides neither general existence and uniqueness nor a
solution for arbitrary initial or boundary conditions, and it does not issue a
Lean-checked proof.

## Appendix 021: omnibias/docs/inverse-pde-map.md

Source: [omnibias/docs/inverse-pde-map.md](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias/docs/inverse-pde-map.md). Original SHA256: `3d409c3bc801791cc96c5a3ef949ad567dcd8f467494955e397767049fd8eeaa`.

This is the complete source note at compilation time. Its original experiment date, protocol, limitations and historical status apply; later corrections in the overview and subsequent audit notes take precedence. Heading levels, line endings, outer document spacing and source-relative Markdown links are normalized here; code and mathematical expressions are preserved.

### Inverting a positive exponential PDE field

The positive Cole–Hopf family in [exact nonlinear PDE identities](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias/docs/nonlinear-pde-identities.md)
connects a nonlinear PDE solution to a finite convex inverse problem. Given a
target velocity, its spatial preimage can be found by matching the mean of a
softmax distribution. The convex geometry supplies a global uniqueness
argument; interval arithmetic can certify a numerical root.

This is an application of classical exponential-family and convex-duality
results. It does not make general nonlinear PDEs linear, make all neural
networks convex, or guarantee rapid convergence near an ill-conditioned target.

#### From the PDE field to a mean map

For fixed spatial modes \(k_j\in\mathbb R^d\), finite real biases \(b_j\),
and viscosity \(\nu>0\), set

\[
\tau(x,t)=\sum_{j=1}^n
\exp\bigl(k_j\cdot x+\nu\lVert k_j\rVert^2t+b_j\bigr),
\qquad U(x,t)=-2\nu\nabla_x\log\tau(x,t).
\]

The sum is nonempty and strictly positive. Each summand satisfies the heat
equation, and the Cole–Hopf identity proves that \(U\) solves the irrotational
vector Burgers system. Biases may vary freely without breaking this identity;
the relation between the temporal and spatial weights must remain intact.

Fix time and write \(a_j=\nu\lVert k_j\rVert^2t+b_j\). Define

\[
Z(x)=\sum_j e^{k_j\cdot x+a_j},\qquad
p_j(x)=\frac{e^{k_j\cdot x+a_j}}{Z(x)},\qquad
\mu(x)=\sum_jp_j(x)k_j.
\]

All \(p_j(x)\) are strictly positive at every finite \(x\). Inverting the
velocity \(U(x,t)=-2\nu m\) is exactly the equation \(\mu(x)=m\). It is
the stationary-point equation of

\[
\Phi_m(x)=\log Z(x)-m\cdot x.
\]

Differentiating the finite sum gives

\[
\nabla\Phi_m(x)=\mu(x)-m,\qquad
C(x):=\nabla^2\Phi_m(x)
=\sum_jp_j(x)(k_j-\mu(x))(k_j-\mu(x))^T.
\]

Thus the Hessian is the covariance matrix of the modes. In particular,
\(D_xU=-2\nu C(x)\) is negative semidefinite. This is a property of this
positive exponential representation; replacing its activation with an arbitrary
function does not preserve the calculation.

For every unit vector \(v\), the scalar values \(v\cdot k_j\) lie in an
interval of length at most \(\operatorname{diam}K\), where
\(K=\operatorname{conv}\{k_1,\ldots,k_n\}\). Subtracting the interval
midpoint shows that their variance is at most one quarter of its squared
length. Consequently,

\[
\lVert C(x)\rVert_2\le\frac{\operatorname{diam}(K)^2}{4},\qquad
\lVert D_xU(x,t)\rVert_2
\le\frac{\nu\operatorname{diam}(K)^2}{2}.
\]

This is a uniform upper bound on spatial sensitivity. It is not a uniform
lower bound on the Hessian or an upper bound on inverse sensitivity.

The hyperplanes \((k_j-k_\ell)\cdot x+a_j-a_\ell=0\) locate equal softmax
weights. Bias changes move these hyperplanes while preserving the PDE family.
The inverse problem uses the whole weighted mean; intersecting equal-weight
hyperplanes alone does not generally solve a prescribed target equation.

#### Exact existence and uniqueness conditions

Assume first that the differences \(k_j-k_1\) span \(\mathbb R^d\).
This is **full affine span**. Ordinary linear rank of the uncentered modes is
insufficient: \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) have linear rank two but affine span one.

For nonzero \(v\),
\[
v^TC(x)v=\operatorname{Var}_{p(x)}(v\cdot k)>0,
\]
because every weight is positive and the projected modes cannot all be equal.
Therefore \(\Phi_m\) is strictly convex on \(\mathbb R^d\). There are three
different target cases:

| Target | Finite preimage and optimization behavior |
| --- | --- |
| \(m\in\operatorname{int}K\) | A unique finite preimage, which is the unique global minimizer of \(\Phi_m\). |
| \(m\in\partial K\) | No finite preimage; the infimum is finite and unattained. Means can approach the target as inputs escape to infinity. |
| \(m\notin K\) | No preimage; \(\Phi_m\) is unbounded below in a separating direction. |

Here is a direct proof of existence in the first case. Choose \(r>0\) with
the ball \(B(m,r)\subset K\). The support function
\(h_K(x)=\max_j k_j\cdot x\) then obeys
\(h_K(x)-m\cdot x\ge r\lVert x\rVert\). Hence

\[
\Phi_m(x)\ge h_K(x)-m\cdot x+\min_j a_j
\ge r\lVert x\rVert+\min_j a_j.
\]

The continuous objective is coercive, so it attains a minimum. The gradient
vanishes there, and strict convexity proves uniqueness.

A finite mean cannot lie on a supporting face: a strictly positive average
attains a supporting linear maximum only when every mode lies on that face,
contradicting full affine span. For a boundary target, any feasible convex
combination gives the finite entropy lower bound below, while evaluation at a
finite input gives a finite upper bound on the infimum. No minimum can be
attained, since an attained minimum would have zero gradient. To see that every
boundary target is a limit of means, approach it through interior targets and
use their preimages. These preimages have no bounded subsequence, since
continuity would otherwise give a finite boundary preimage.

For an exterior target, strict separation gives a vector \(v\) with
\(m\cdot v>h_K(v)\). For \(s>0\),
\[
\Phi_m(sv)\le s\bigl(h_K(v)-m\cdot v\bigr)
                  +\max_j a_j+\log n\longrightarrow-\infty.
\]

If the modes have a deficient affine span, let
\(L=\operatorname{span}\{k_j-k_1\}\). The range of the mean map is
\(\operatorname{relint}K\). For a target in that relative interior there is
one solution modulo \(L^\perp\): adding a vector in \(L^\perp\) shifts all
logits equally and changes neither probabilities nor the mean. The objective
is also unchanged when \(m\in\operatorname{aff}K\). Any implementation that
returns a unique input must fix a gauge or explicitly require full affine span.
Duplicate modes are allowed; finite biases still give each duplicate positive
mass. Removing a mode, for example through an idealized bias of \(-\infty\),
changes the convex hull and is a different problem.

These statements specialize the mean-parameter results in
[Wainwright and Jordan, *Graphical Models, Exponential Families, and Variational
Inference*](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~jordan/sail/readings/wainwright-jordan-fnt.pdf),
Sections 3.5–3.6 and Appendix B. In that author-hosted version, Proposition 2
gives the covariance Hessian, Proposition 3 gives injectivity under minimality,
and Theorem 1 gives surjectivity onto the interior. Minimality here is exactly
the affine-span condition.

#### Rational witnesses and a global objective bound

For rational modes and a rational target, a proposed vector \(q\) can be checked
using exact rational arithmetic:

\[
q_j\ge0,\qquad \sum_jq_j=1,\qquad \sum_jq_jk_j=m.
\]

This proves membership in \(K\). If every \(q_j>0\), full affine span proves
interior membership: a supporting equality at \(m\) would force equality at
every mode. An exact positive witness can therefore establish existence before
the numerical inverse solve. A zero component does not prove that the target
is on the boundary; another representation may have all positive components.
Approximate feasibility within a floating-point tolerance is not this exact
witness.

Every feasible \(q\), including those with zero components, gives

\[
B(q)=\sum_jq_ja_j-\sum_{j:q_j>0}q_j\log q_j
\le\inf_x\Phi_m(x).
\]

The omitted zero terms use \(0\log0=0\). Indeed, substituting the softmax
formula and using the exact moment constraints gives

\[
\Phi_m(x)-B(q)
=\sum_{j:q_j>0}q_j\log\frac{q_j}{p_j(x)}
=\operatorname{KL}(q\Vert p(x))\ge0.
\]

Thus an interval lower bound for \(B(q)\) and an interval upper bound for
\(\Phi_m\) at any finite witness yield a global minimum-value enclosure.
The logarithms require rigorous transcendental enclosures. Exact rational
feasibility alone does not make the entropy rational, nor does it make the
bound tight. In an interior problem equality holds when \(q=p(x_*)\); a fixed
feasible witness can remain loose even after the numerical input converges.

#### Certification and conditioning

A stable numerical solve can propose an input using the gradient and covariance
matrix. Subtracting a common logit before exponentiation avoids many overflow
problems, but does not itself certify the result. Floating-point underflow can
turn a positive probability into numerical zero, and very large dot products
can overflow before the shift. Such numerical failures must not be interpreted
as a proof that a target is on a face or outside the convex hull.

The verified path encloses the residual \(F(x)=\mu(x)-m\) and its Jacobian
\(C(x)\) on a box. A successful Krawczyk test proves that a true zero exists
inside an explicit enclosure. Full affine span then upgrades this local root
claim to the unique global minimizer of \(\Phi_m\). This uses the existing
multidimensional Krawczyk primitive; it does not require a global box search.
Failure of the interval test is inconclusive. It cannot negate an exact
interior witness or establish boundary/exterior membership.

At an interior target the implicit function theorem gives the inverse
derivatives

\[
D_mx_*=C(x_*)^{-1},\qquad
\frac{\partial x_*}{\partial a_j}
=-C(x_*)^{-1}p_j(x_*)(k_j-m).
\]

For a fixed target and the heat-dispersion biases
\(a_j(t)=\nu\lVert k_j\rVert^2t+b_j\), this also gives

\[
\frac{d x_*}{dt}
=-\nu C(x_*)^{-1}
\operatorname{Cov}_{p(x_*)}(k,\lVert k\rVert^2).
\]

These are identities for the exact solution. Evaluating them at an approximate
input produces numerical sensitivities unless the input and matrix solve are
enclosed separately. No global lower eigenvalue bound follows from full affine
span: probabilities may concentrate as the input tends to infinity, making
the covariance nearly singular. A small residual alone therefore does not
provide a small distance-to-solution bound. This matters especially near the
boundary of the target hull.

#### Exact model and verified API

`omnibias.core.verified.mean_map.MeanMap(modes, biases, target, budget=None)`
stores a frozen exact model. Entries are integers or `Fraction` objects, with
one bias per mode and one target coordinate per spatial dimension. Its
`dimension`, `mode_count` and `affine_rank` properties describe the checked
model; `affine_rank` is computed from the mode differences using exact
arithmetic. The optional resource budget is a `RidgeBudget`.

| Method | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `objective(box)` | Encloses \(\Phi_m\) over the supplied interval box. |
| `residual(box)` | Encloses every coordinate of \(\mu-m\). |
| `jacobian(box)` | Encloses every covariance-matrix entry. |
| `dual_bound(weights)` | Checks exact feasibility of \(q\), then encloses \(B(q)\). Invalid mathematical witnesses raise `ValueError`. |
| `target_interior(weights)` | Checks strict positivity, exact feasibility and full affine rank. A false result is inconclusive about hull membership. |
| `float_evaluate(point)` | Returns untrusted original and common-bias-reduced objectives, a residual and a covariance for proposing an iterate. |

`target_interior` returns false for invalid mathematical witnesses or deficient
rank; malformed types, shapes and exceeded budgets still raise. A failed
witness is not a separating hyperplane. The model's transcendental interval
evaluations require the rigorous backend, available through
`omnibias-core[verified]`.

Exact common mode and bias offsets are removed before numerical evaluation.
The proposal's `reduced_objective` excludes the first bias, so a large common
constant does not erase small descent differences. The original objective
still has to fit the numerical range for `float_evaluate` to succeed. If it
does not, the iterative solver can return `"not_certified"` even when the
residual and Jacobian remain evaluable for a direct root check.

For a small example, take modes \(0,e_1,e_2\), biases \((0,-1,1)\), and
target \((1/3,1/3)\). At \(x_*=(1,-1)\) all three logits vanish, so the
uniform weights give the target exactly. The following code asks the solver
to find and certify that input, starting from its default zero proposal.

```python
from fractions import Fraction

from omnibias.core.verified.interval import Interval
from omnibias.core.verified.inverse_mean_map import inverse_mean_map
from omnibias.core.verified.linalg import interval_solve
from omnibias.core.verified.mean_map import MeanMap

third = Fraction(1, 3)
model = MeanMap(
    ((0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1)),
    (0, -1, 1),
    (third, third),
)
q = (third, third, third)
assert model.affine_rank == model.dimension == 2
assert model.target_interior(q)

result = inverse_mean_map(model)
assert result.status == "certified"
certificate = result.certificate
assert certificate is not None
assert certificate.enclosure[0].contains(1.0)
assert certificate.enclosure[1].contains(-1.0)

# A separate global minimum-value enclosure from primal and dual witnesses.
lower = model.dual_bound(q)
upper = model.objective(tuple(Interval.point(x) for x in result.point))
minimum = Interval(lower.lo, upper.hi)
print(result.point, certificate.enclosure, minimum)

# First column of D_target x*: C(x*) inverse times the first unit vector.
column = interval_solve(model.jacobian(certificate.enclosure), (1, 0))
assert column[0].contains(6.0)
assert column[1].contains(3.0)
```

Here the exact minimum value is \(\log3\). The root certificate establishes
location and uniqueness; `minimum` is a separate value enclosure. Because
\(q=p(x_*)\) in this example, the entropy lower bound is optimal. The exact
inverse covariance is \(\begin{pmatrix}6&3\\3&6\end{pmatrix}\).
`interval_solve` verifies its own matrix enclosure conditions and raises when
they are inconclusive. A certified inverse point does not by itself guarantee
that an arbitrary-width interval sensitivity solve will succeed.

`inverse_mean_map` and `certify_mean_inverse` are imported from
`omnibias.core.verified.inverse_mean_map`.
`inverse_mean_map(model, initial=None, max_iterations=64, radii=...)` proposes
an input and tries a finite list of certificate radii. The default radii are
`(1e-8, 1e-6, 1e-4, 1e-2)`. Success stops at the first proven root enclosure.
The returned `point` remains an approximate center; no residual or position
tolerance is implied. Use `certificate.enclosure` for the proved root location.
Restricting the radius list, for example to `radii=(1e-8,)`, asks the checker
to certify a smaller tested box and can make a finite search inconclusive.
The returned result has `point`, `iterations`, `certificate`, and one of these
statuses:

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `"certified"` | A verified root enclosure and exact full affine rank establish the unique global minimizer. |
| `"not_certified"` | The computation did not produce that certificate. The proposed point carries no root or global-minimum guarantee. |
| `"rank_deficient"` | The modes fail the full affine-span requirement. The implementation does not choose a quotient gauge. |

The iteration budget and finite radius list do not guarantee certification of
every interior target. `"not_certified"` does not classify the target as
boundary or exterior. Likewise, `"rank_deficient"` does not prove that no
preimage exists.

For a proposed point and approximate inverse Jacobian,
`certify_mean_inverse(model, point, preconditioner, radius)` attempts the same
verified check directly. It returns a `MeanInverseCertificate` or `None`.
The certificate contains the proposal `point`, the actual tested interval
`box`, the tighter root `enclosure`, exact `affine_rank`, contraction bound
`kappa`, and a serialized `certificate`. These are interval-arithmetic claims;
they do not assert verification by the Lean kernel. The sensitivity identities
above currently have no dedicated sensitivity API.

#### Scope

The mathematical model, numerical proposal, exact witness and interval root
enclosure have different roles. The root and objective claims concern the
ideal real-valued exponential model with the declared exact constants, not an
arbitrary hardware forward pass.

This inverse problem finds a spatial input at a fixed time and fixed biases.
It does not fit arbitrary PDE data, impose initial or boundary conditions, or
train an unrestricted neural network. The construction assumes the previously
verified Cole–Hopf solution family; solving its mean equation establishes the
requested velocity preimage within that family. Its convex geometry and
entropy duality are classical. The reusable capability is their integration
with exact model data, explicit witness checks and verified root enclosures.

The numerical distinction between shifted formulas and mathematical guarantees
is discussed in [Blanchard, Higham and Higham, *Accurate Computation of the
Log-Sum-Exp and Softmax Functions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.03469). No universal
iteration bound, floating-point identity across backends, or formal Lean
verification is implied by this construction.

## Appendix 022: omnibias-lab/README.md

Source: [omnibias-lab/README.md](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/README.md). Original SHA256: `d3aeadd4fdc91e4d6a645cb3167253ce28b3b6b6f31e9ee171d6084e5f7834f2`.

This is the complete source note at compilation time. Its original experiment date, protocol, limitations and historical status apply; later corrections in the overview and subsequent audit notes take precedence. Heading levels, line endings, outer document spacing and source-relative Markdown links are normalized here; code and mathematical expressions are preserved.

### omnibias-lab

An isolated research environment for modern derivative comparisons,
complete nonlinear boundary-value certificates and gauge-spectrum validation.
It consumes the adjacent omnibias checkout through editable paths. Reusable
math lives in omnibias; the all-spin SU(2) proof and campaign live in ensemble-laws.

Read the [research note and claim-to-evidence table](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/docs/research-note.md),
[PDE proof](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/docs/pde-certificate.md), [directional benchmark report](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/docs/directional-benchmarks.md),
and [unshipped stability experiment](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/stability/README.md).

The strongest measured result here is **7.96× faster neural verification** at
the same proved error, using a fifth-derivative bound. The separate two-plaquette
SU(2) calculation includes every spin and encloses its dimensionless gap to
under 0.12% width at the stated coupling. The classical Chebyshev PDE baseline
still wins overall. No scientific novelty or continuum Yang–Mills claim is made.

The [multi-bias frontier prototype](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/multibias_frontier_research/README.md)
contains the completed bounded activation-growth, pretrained-compression and
maximum-margin-band study. Its evidence report distinguishes a narrow fresh
synthetic-band result from the failed primary advancement gates.

#### Reproduce

Place `omnibias-lab`, `omnibias` and `ensemble-laws` beside one another.
Use Python 3.14 and the lockfile. The optional plots extra is needed only for
the exported figure. Private ensemble data are not needed for these pilots.

```bash
uv sync --locked --extra plots
uv run --extra plots python -m benchmarks.bootstrap_stde
uv run --extra plots pytest
uv run --extra plots python -m pde.run
uv run --extra plots python -m benchmarks.run_matrix directional --output artifacts/reproduction_directional
uv run --extra plots python -m benchmarks.run_matrix operators --output artifacts/reproduction_operators
uv run --extra plots python -m benchmarks.manifest
```

From `../ensemble-laws`, reproduce the complete spin bounds:

```bash
uv run python -m ensemble_laws.full_spin --kappa-lower 1 --two-j-max 6 --steps 12 --output artifacts/full_spin_kappa1_cut6.json
uv run python -m ensemble_laws.full_spin --kappa-lower 99/100 --kappa-upper 101/100 --two-j-max 6 --steps 12 --output artifacts/full_spin_kappa_interval_cut6.json
uv run pytest tests/test_full_spin.py
```

Use `--output` beneath `$OMNIBIAS_SCRATCH/ensemble-laws` instead if a scratch
directory is configured. Default command outputs honor scratch automatically.
The stored publication figure can be regenerated in this lab with
`uv run --extra plots python -m reports.pilot_figure`; it reads the separately
recorded accuracy pilot, PDE summary and named full-spin artifacts.

`run_matrix` runs cases serially in separate processes, enforces deadlines and
process-tree memory limits, and retains errors. A whole matrix is a multi-minute
run. `--resume` now requires matching command, source, dependencies and lockfile;
the historical first-run artifacts predate that guard and are deliberately
refused for resume. Their source manifest was captured after the runs. Fresh
reproduction directories avoid mixing those histories.

#### Evidence and limits

The first main matrices recorded 34/36 directional passes and 23 operator
evaluations (17 deterministic passes, six stochastic error reports). Failures,
setup time, gradient cost, input digests and software versions are in the JSON.
These single-machine, one-seed matrices are pilots, not general performance
claims. [Benchmark details](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/docs/directional-benchmarks.md).

The corrected PDE run has six passing, replayed certificates. Its functional
analysis is proved in writing, and its finite gates are independently recomputed.
Neither a certificate digest nor the use of mpmath constitutes a Lean build.
The corrected directed transcendental backend and its explicit special-function
remainders are described in `../omnibias/docs/transcend-soundness.md`.

Final focused validation: 88 lab tests, 531 core/interval/Green tests, and
58 distinct spectral/replay/CLI tests passed across the final focused runs.
Earlier consumer regressions also passed after the
recoupling change. These are targeted checks, not a claim that the entire
omnibias monorepo test suite was run.

Large generated outputs stay in `artifacts/` or the configured scratch directory.
The [research program](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/ensemble-laws/docs/breakthrough-program.md) records
remaining targets, including independent reproduction and the open Clay obligations.

#### Positive-source Poisson compression

The [complete source-compression pilot](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/docs/source-compression.md) adds an exact
maximum-norm error controller for merging positive point forces. It includes
Green-function, fitted-FEM, coarse-FEM and adaptive-spline controls. All six
accuracy cases pass; classical Green interpolation is 10.5–30.8 times faster
for one solve, and no warm-query speed advantage is established. The weak
Gaussian source bound from the earlier pilot does not imply a PDE solution bound.

#### Oblique-band tabular pilot

The [frozen band-model comparison](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/tabular/README.md) contains six datasets, three
split seeds and seven model families. The band model has the best mean test
log loss on none of these datasets; it remains competitive in some small tasks.
All 378 attempts, including six failed QDA trials, are retained. The separate
optional comparator environment and the limits are documented with the results.

#### Higher-moment geometry study

The [spectral study](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/tabular/SPECTRAL_RESULTS.md) adds 819 trial attempts across
fresh Gaussian tasks, Ionosphere and Sonar. Fourth-order initialization improves
both collapsed and Gaussian models on balanced XOR. Real-data results are mixed;
this does not establish a collapse-specific or novel learning method. The frozen
protocol, independent mathematical checks and baseline repairs are retained.

The [Hermite geometry and matrix-kernel follow-up](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/tabular/USTAT_RESULTS.md) records the full literature estimator, all 168 fresh-data test evaluations, equivalent pair/tensor timing controls and training-only radial-score diagnostics.

The [fitted-density fresh-data study](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/tabular/DENSITY_RESULTS.md) adds 510 successful evaluations, five fresh draws per task, unknown tail/ellipse parameters and equally initialized conventional profiles.

The [stronger profile controls](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/tabular/PROFILE_RESULTS.md) add 360 fresh evaluations: learned Laplace beats learned collapsed on all six means and 29/30 pairs.

The [metric-expectation reference](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/tabular/METRIC_EXPECTATION.md) gives a variance enclosure, differentiable exact-expectation prototype, 810 numerical checks and an explicitly classical LP connection.

The LP/F1 bridge (`tabular/metric_lp_bridge.py`) uses Charnes–Cooper, exact
rational witness checks and the substrate's verified LP dual bound. Its frozen
76-case audit retains nonzero expected-optimum gaps: it does not turn exact
expected F1 into an LP. The repaired substrate check rejects interval-overlap
as a proof of equality feasibility. The main research record is
`../omnibias/docs/bias-collapse-pde.md`.

With the locked optional tabular environment and the lab root on `PYTHONPATH`:

```bash
python -m tabular.metric_lp_audit --output artifacts/metric_lp_audit.json
python -m tabular.metric_lp_audit --output artifacts/metric_lp_audit.json --verify-only
python -m tabular.metric_lp_report --input artifacts/metric_lp_audit.json
python -m pytest tests/test_metric_lp_bridge.py tests/test_metric_lp_audit.py tests/test_metric_expectation.py -q
```

Resume requires the original resolved output path, source hashes, command and
pinned dependency/lock state. The report separately checks the full matrix,
metadata and analytic oracles. Neither replay nor the report invokes the LP
optimizer. The pre-import-format artifact and its source are retained under
`artifacts/metric_lp_before_import_sort/`.

The matched rare-positive learning study (`tabular/metric_learning_study.py`)
compares six objectives in the same linear-logit family with validation-tuned
thresholds. It records 180 selections and 630 optimizer fits. Expected F1 has
no strictly higher case mean than ordinary BCE in this final-point recipe;
validation checkpoints and newer metric-specific methods remain open controls.
The replayer recomputes selection, training objectives and held-out scores.

```bash
python -m tabular.metric_learning_study --output artifacts/metric_learning_study.json --data-dir /path/to/public-data
python -m tabular.metric_learning_study --output artifacts/metric_learning_study.json --data-dir /path/to/public-data --verify-only
```

The separate rounding prototype (`tabular/metric_rounding.py`) applies
coordinate coupling bounds to nearly certain Bernoulli predictions. It has

### Projection sharing with learned profiles: proof obligations and sources

Registered 20 October 2026. These are complete elementary arguments supporting
the prototype. Their use here is not a claim that the ingredients are new.

#### 1. The representation being compressed

Let a shallow sigmoid block be
f_o(x) = d_o + sum_j C_oj sigmoid(w_j^T x + b_j).
Grouping directions replaces w_j by v_g(j), retaining all individual biases
and output coefficients. Equality of grouped directions gives exact equality
of the real functions. The deployed model stores R directions, H biases,
O*H coefficients, O offsets and H group indices. It still evaluates H scalar
sigmoids. Vector output profiles are necessary for arbitrary multiclass C.

This is a shared-weight ridge-function representation. It is more general
than the ordered fixed-alternating Boolean unit, and its conclusions must
not be transferred to that restricted class without proof.

#### 2. Direction, bias, readout and deletion bound

Assume |x_i| <= r, finite parameters, sigmoid s with 0 <= s <= 1 and
|s'| <= 1/4. Match retained student terms to distinct original teacher terms.
For a matched pair j,k, write

C_t s(a_t) - C_s s(a_s)
= C_t [s(a_t)-s(a_s)] + (C_t-C_s)s(a_s).

Consequently its absolute contribution to output o is at most

|C_t| min(1, (r ||w_t-v_s||_1 + |b_t-b_s|)/4) + |C_t-C_s|.

Add |d_t-d_s|, |C_t| for each deleted original term, and |C_s| for each new
student term. The triangle inequality proves the implemented uniform bound
on the whole input box. New terms have source identity -1; retained identities
must be unique. The certificate constructor and checker organize these sums
differently and use exact Fraction arithmetic on stored float32 dyadics.

The statement bounds real functions with those parameters. It does not include
floating-point inference rounding error. A large valid bound can be useless;
the checker therefore does not automatically certify label preservation.
If an independently proved teacher margin between the top logit p and every
other logit q exceeds E_p+E_q, labels are preserved. Empirical margins alone
do not prove this condition for all inputs.

For a subsequent fixed affine map B followed by coordinatewise L-Lipschitz
activation, coordinate errors propagate as E_new <= L |B| E. Repeat this
operation through a fixed tail. Changes to that tail need additional error
terms; the current deep-distillation study makes no global certificate claim.

#### 3. Adjacent-pair pruning

For a<b, s(z-a)-s(z-b) = sinh(h)/(cosh(t)+cosh(h)),
where h=(b-a)/2 and t=z-(a+b)/2. The denominator is minimized at t=0,
so the exact supremum is tanh((b-a)/4).

For arbitrary scalar coefficients c1,c2, put u=(c1-c2)/2 and v=(c1+c2)/2.
Then c1*s1+c2*s2 = u*(s1-s2)+v*(s1+s2), implying a deletion error at most
|u| tanh(|b1-b2|/4) + |c1+c2|. Apply this coordinatewise for vector coefficients.
The rational checker uses tanh(t) <= min(1,t), t>=0. The result remains valid
when coefficients are unequal or have the same sign; the bound can then be
too large to permit pruning. Bias proximity by itself is insufficient.

#### 4. Function-preserving growth and optimizer coordinates

Adding a term with zero output coefficients leaves the initial function
unchanged. Its coefficient Jacobian is the proposed sigmoid feature; its
bias Jacobian is initially zero. Thus this construction supplies a new
coefficient direction, not an immediate nonzero gradient for every parameter.

If F_tilde(theta,0)=F(theta) for every theta and the original parameter metric
is retained, the extended Jacobian is [J_theta, J_gamma]. For squared loss
L=||F-y||^2/2, Euclidean gradient flow gives

-dL_extended/dt = -dL_original/dt + ||J_gamma^T(F-y)||^2

at insertion. This is an instantaneous statement. It proves no general
finite-step speedup, convergence, or held-out improvement. For cross entropy,
the analogous score uses the logit-loss gradient. Validation accepts or rejects
trial updates; rejected trials are counted in the computational budget.

Adam's old first/second moments and step counts must survive insertion.
New coordinates start with zero moments. Deleting terms selects the matching
old moments. Rebuilding Adam without that migration would confound the study.

The default even-K all-plus mean at equal biases has equal bias derivatives.
Symmetric deterministic updates preserve equality, so that activation remains
a single shifted sigmoid despite having multiple stored biases. This is a
specific initialization limitation, not a failure of independent signed units.

#### 5. Conditions for replacing depth

Let f(X) be square-integrable and Z=v^T X. Write m(Z)=E[f|Z]. Orthogonality
E[(f-m(Z))h(Z)]=0 gives, for every square-integrable profile g,

E[(f-g(Z))^2] = E[Var(f|Z)] + E[(m(Z)-g(Z))^2].

Taking the infimum over a specified profile class G_K proves the proposed
decomposition. An injective projection of a finite dataset makes the first
term zero for unrestricted measurable g, so a meaningful compression claim
must retain the complexity/regularity/precision restriction and unseen data.

For X uniform on [-1,1]^2 and the specified projection Z=X1, f=X1*X2 has
E[f|Z]=0 and irreducible MSE E[X1^2]E[X2^2]=1/9. More broadly, smooth scalar
ridge functions have Hessian rank at most one; X1*X2 has Hessian rank two.
These distinguish genuine information loss from an optimization failure.

An analytic positive fixture is
f(x)=2*s(6*(s(3*x1)-1/2))-1.
It contains a composition but depends on one projection. A shallow richer
profile may approximate it; finite fitting alone is not an exact symbolic
identity or a universal depth-reduction theorem. Its padded implementation is
a manufactured fixture and is excluded from competitive promotion.

#### 6. Prior art and contribution boundaries

- Kim et al., NeurIPS 2020, *Neuron Merging: Compensating for Pruned Neurons*:
  https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2020/hash/0678ca2eae02d542cc931e81b74de122-Abstract.html
  Merging and compensating discarded neurons are established. Our direction
  sharing retains separate scalar profiles and still needs comparative evidence.
- Kuniya and Ohkubo, submitted 1 October 2026, *Neuron merging via inverse-
  activation regression for post-training compression of sigmoid neural networks*:
  https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02559
  Close current work uses clustering and inverse-activation least squares.
  The pilot adds a local, labelled averaged-activation inverse-regression control;
  it is not an official reproduction or an exact copy of their method.
- Unser 2019, *A Representer Theorem for Deep Neural Networks*:
  https://jmlr.org/papers/v20/18-418.html
  Learned spline activations and complexity regularization have explicit theory.
  The local bounded-knot spline control tests representation/implementation effects.
- Chen et al., *Net2Net*: https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.05641
  Function-preserving expansion predates the proposed growth heuristic.
- Duch 2006, *K-Separability*: https://is.umk.pl/~duch/pubs/06-k-rep-LNCS.pdf
  Multiple intervals on one projection, model selection and separation margins
  are established. Boolean completeness is not the compression novelty claim.

A potentially new contribution would need a specific stronger guarantee,
algorithmic result or independently confirmed competitive architecture beyond
these ingredients. This eight-hour pilot evaluates the computational case.

This is the complete source note at compilation time. ### Exhaustive minimum-transition audit, n = 1, 2, 3, 4

This experiment certifies the worst-case minimum number of label transitions along an injective linear projection of Boolean-cube vertices. It is a statement about projection/staircase representation, not optimization success and not a general architecture novelty claim.

Let V_n = {0,1}^n. For a labeling f and weight w with distinct scores, let pi_w sort w dot x. Define

    b(f) = min_w sum_(i=1)^(2^n-1) [f(pi_w(i)) != f(pi_w(i+1))].
    B(n) = max_f b(f).

One hard threshold step is needed at each transition, with a free initial output level/complement convention. A finite shared-slope sigmoid construction approximates these steps sufficiently closely to classify the finite cube exactly at a threshold when the ordered score margins are positive. Counting constant offsets or forcing a particular tail/output convention requires separate accounting.

The exact exhaustive results are B(1)=1, B(2)=2, B(3)=3, B(4)=5. No closed form for general n is claimed.

| n | Fundamental-sector chambers | All projection orders | NPN classes | Worst minimum |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|1|1|2|2|1|
|2|1|8|4|2|
|3|2|96|14|3|
|4|14|5376|222|5|

For n=4, the distribution over all 65,536 truth tables is: 2 require 0 transitions, 1,880 require 1, 14,244 require 2, 30,216 require 3, 19,002 require 4, and 192 require 5. Worst NPN representatives are integers 1785 and 7140. Bit i of f labels vertex i, whose coordinates are the n-bit binary expansion with most significant coordinate first. For example, n=2 uses 00,01,10,11 in that order.

#### Completeness argument

Every two distinct cube vertices differ by d in {-1,0,1}^n. Their scores exchange order only on d dot w = 0. Retain one normal from each pair d,-d by requiring its first nonzero coordinate to be positive. There are (3^n-1)/2 such distinct hyperplanes.

Signed coordinate permutations preserve the cube, up to an additive constant in projected scores. Every generic w can therefore be moved into the open fundamental sector 0 < w_0 < ... < w_(n-1). The sector inequalities are S w > 0, with S row 0 = e_0 and row i = e_i-e_(i-1).

A chamber sign vector s is feasible exactly when the homogeneous strict system s_j d_j dot w > 0 and S w > 0 is feasible. Because there are finitely many inequalities, homogeneity lets us replace all right-hand sides by 1: B w >= 1. LP finds candidates, but its numerical status is not trusted alone:

* A feasible candidate is rationalized and every inequality B_i dot w >= 1 is checked using Fraction arithmetic.
* An infeasible candidate is accompanied by nonnegative rational y with sum y = 1 and B^T y = 0. If B w >= 1 held, then 0 = y^T B w >= sum y = 1, a contradiction. Every such certificate is verified exactly.

The enumeration starts in the chamber containing (1,3,9,...). Each chamber's every one-sign-flip neighbor is either enumerated as feasible or carries the exact infeasibility certificate above. The adjacency graph of chambers of a finite hyperplane arrangement restricted to an open convex sector is connected: a generic path joining two interior points crosses one arrangement hyperplane at a time and avoids intersections of two distinct hyperplanes. Thus the closed explored component is the entire chamber set. Equality of multiple vertex pairs caused by the same d is handled together by its single sign, not by an invalid individual adjacent-vertex swap.

A successful representation with tied scores cannot benefit from tying differently labeled points. When each tied block has constant label, sufficiently small generic perturbation separates points within the block while preserving all between-block score orders, adding no transitions. Therefore restricting to generic weights does not increase the optimum.

For each sector chamber, exact rational weights give a distinct total order. Apply all n! coordinate permutations and 2^n input complements to recover every generic order. NPN classes further quotient truth tables by those input symmetries and output complementation, all of which preserve the minimum transition count. The replayer explicitly partitions all 2^(2^n) truth tables into the listed disjoint orbits and evaluates every full projection order on every representative. No sampled directions enter the n<=4 proof.

#### Independent replay and fingerprints

The generator uses NumPy and SciPy/HiGHS for proposing primal and dual certificates. The replayer uses only the Python standard library, independently recomputing all rational certificates, closure of the chamber list under feasible neighbors, vertex orders, signed-permutation orbits and exact transition minima. Its source and the generator source, dependency versions, configuration, timing boundaries, and artifact digests are recorded in manifest.json. The generator refuses an existing output directory.

    OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 \
      /tmp/omnibias-geometry-comparators/bin/python enumerate_orders.py --output <fresh-directory>
    /tmp/omnibias-geometry-comparators/bin/python replay_orders.py --output <directory>

The separately retained n5_exact_counterexample.json concerns one supplied five-input label vector, under the explicitly recorded lexicographic bit ordering. Integer weights [17,979,753,578,971] realize that vector with only three transitions, at thresholds 761.5, 1736.5 and 2711.5. It is not a computation of B(5), and a different input/label convention must be converted before comparing to another table.

#### Fixed alternating signs and no output offset

For the convention F(z)=H(z-t1)-H(z-t2)+H(z-t3)-... with ordered thresholds and fixed readout at 1/2, the count for an observed vertex order is K = transitions + first_label. A first positive observed label requires an initial step before the first observed score. Thus output complementation is not free.

The separately fingerprinted fixed_sign_audit.py exhaustively enumerates NP orbits without output complementation. fixed_sign_replay.py independently checks all orbits and minima using standard-library integer arithmetic; the base arrangement certificates are replayed by replay_orders.py. Both checks passed. The worst-case values remain 1,2,3,5 for n=1,2,3,4, respectively, but the truth-table distributions differ:

| n | NP classes | Counts by minimum biases |
|---|---:|---|
|1|3|0:1, 1:3|
|2|6|0:1, 1:13, 2:2|
|3|22|0:1, 1:103, 2:106, 3:46|
|4|402|0:1, 1:1881, 2:9248, 3:35212, 4:18330, 5:864|

    python fixed_sign_audit.py --base <base-artifacts> --output <fresh-fixed-sign-directory>
    python fixed_sign_replay.py --base <base-artifacts> --output <fixed-sign-directory>

For the supplied n=5 function, the paper's alternative convention uses coordinates x_k = +1 iff bit k is set, otherwise -1, with least-significant coordinate first. The integer weights become [971,578,753,979,17] and thresholds become [-1775,175,2125]. The exact margin is 9, so the three-logistic sum at beta=1 also correctly classifies every input: absolute deviation from the hard prefix sum is at most 3 exp(-9) < 1/2. This check is included in replay_n5_counterexample.py. It disproves an eight-bias lower bound for this particular printed function under those conventions; it does not settle the worst case B(5).

#### Five-input lower-bound witness

A separate exact enumeration for n=5 finds 516 chambers in the sorted positive sector and 1,981,440 full projection orders. To reduce LP work, discard normals whose hyperplanes cannot intersect that sector: writing w_i = sum_(j<=i) u_j with every u_j>0 gives d dot w = sum_j (sum_(i>=j)d_i)u_j. This can be zero in the sector exactly when the suffix sums contain both a positive and a negative value. Exactly 26 normals survive. All 516 feasible rational witnesses and 9,659 infeasible-neighbor certificates replay exactly.

The fixed no-offset convention was evaluated on a sample of 50 truth tables (seed 20261021); the largest encountered minimum was seven. The selected witness integer 3350833497 was then rerun and independently replayed against all 1,981,440 orders. Its exact minimum is seven, including the first-label startup cost. This proves B0(5)>=7. It does not prove B0(5)=7, B0(5)=8, or a universal upper bound below the elementary bound 32.

    python enumerate_n5.py --output <fresh-n5-directory>
    python replay_n5.py --output <n5-directory>

The independent n5 replay uses only the standard library and passed in approximately eight seconds. These scripts and the selected witness are separately fingerprinted. The initial attempt to make the n5 generator portable failed before chamber enumeration due to an accidental code-generation replacement inside the rationalization helper. The helper was corrected; the final generator and independent replayer were then rerun from a fresh directory. No failed run contributed a mathematical result.

This is the complete source note at compilation time. Its original experiment date, protocol, limitations and historical status apply; later corrections in the overview and subsequent audit notes take precedence. Heading levels, line endings, outer document spacing and source-relative Markdown links are normalized here; code and mathematical expressions are preserved.

### Unshipped continuous-bias certificate pilot

Atoms are `psi_b(x) = max(x-b,0)^2`, with fixed direction 1 and rational bias
in a compact interval. The optimization fits finite point moments and minimizes
the signed coefficient total variation. It does not solve a PDE or bound
unobserved function error. The optional weak interpretation is the classical
distributional identity `D_x^3 psi_b = 2 delta_b`.

No unpenalized polynomial nullspace is included. Consequently the represented
field and its first two derivatives vanish to the left of the allowed bias
interval. This is a specific causal Green representation, with normalization
factor 2, rather than the full family of quadratic splines with arbitrary
polynomial boundary data. Its source total variation is twice the atom cost.

For rational dual q, `g(b)=sum_i q_i psi_b(x_i)` is quadratic on every interval
between consecutive data knots. Write it as `A b^2-2 B b+C`. A nonzero quadratic
has its only stationary point at `b=B/A`; a linear/constant polynomial needs
only its interval endpoints. Since maxima of `|g|` occur at endpoints or
stationary points of g, this finite rational candidate list proves the global
price `U=max_b |g(b)|`. It covers every permitted continuous bias, not merely
a grid. For U>0, q/U is dual feasible for

    min_mu ||mu||TV subject to integral psi_b(x_i) dmu(b) = y_i.

Its exact lower bound is `q.y/U`. Any exactly feasible finite atom list gives
an upper bound `sum_b |a_b|`, after combining duplicate biases. An exhausted
resource bound or failed exact reconstruction supplies no certificate. A
known target-generating atom list may be used as an explicitly labeled feasible
upper bound; it is not an independently recovered solution.

The inequality follows directly from weak duality:
`q.y = integral g(b) dmu(b) <= ||g||infinity ||mu||TV`.
It does not require strong duality, existence of a continuous minimizer, or
convergence of the exchange method. If U=0 and q.y=0, q is already feasible;
if U=0 and q.y is nonzero, scaling q gives a Farkas-style witness that the
point-moment target is infeasible for the whole continuous dictionary. The
feasible-target pilot refuses that contradictory case explicitly.

The interior example `x=(1,2), q=(-3,1), b in [0,1]` gives
`g(b)=-2b^2+2b+1`, so endpoint-only pricing reports 1 while the true price is
3/2 at b=1/2. For target `(1/4,9/4)`, the endpoint dictionary has optimum 3/2;
the continuous dictionary has optimum 1, certified by the single atom b=1/2
and the rescaled dual. This disproves a *continuous* certificate inferred only
from finite-grid dual feasibility.

The mathematics is established spline/convex-measure optimization. Relevant
primary sources are [Parhi and Nowak 2021](https://jmlr.org/papers/v22/20-583.html),
[Bach 2017](https://jmlr.org/papers/v18/14-546.html), and
[Pilanci and Ergen 2020](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v119/pilanci20a.html).
Column generation with an exact pricing oracle is a classical exchange method.
For a recovered interior primal atom, a continuous optimum must additionally
satisfy `g(b)=sign(a)` and `g'(b)=0`. The driver can reconstruct a rational dual
from these linear equations; the exact global pricing step then independently
checks it. This does not use the known target-generating atoms. Inconsistent or
unhelpful stationarity candidates are retained and do not produce a pass.
This prototype checks a narrow continuous-dictionary primal/dual gap, which the
existing distributional ridge evaluator alone does not provide. It does not
establish novel mathematics or a speed advantage.

Run the frozen small matrix with the repository environment, one CPU thread:

    OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 \
      /home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias/.venv/bin/python run.py --output result.json

Replay every retained exact claim without linprog or retiming:

    /home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias/.venv/bin/python replay.py result.json

Replay independently rebuilds every pricing cell and its extrema, exact primal
residuals, scaled dual feasibility, bounds and gaps, including all seven cases,
fresh seeds 101/211/307, exchange transitions and dense grids 21/101. It checks
the six source-file hashes, dependency versions, installed RECORD manifests,
selected NumPy/SciPy runtime byte hashes, the Python executable and shared exact
elimination source. This is explicit provenance coverage, not a hash of every
dependency byte. Recorded solver status and wall time are observations and are
not independently established by replay. Tampering tests cover false grid
maxima, altered cells/gaps, missing cases/controls, stale hashes and unsupported
primal/dual claims.
