### Exact nesting can preserve different amounts of trainable tangent freedom

Read-only mathematical followup. No image package, frozen recipe, source snapshot or training run was changed. Reproducible independent NumPy checks: `/tmp/nesting_tangent_probe.py` and `/tmp/nesting_tangent_probe.json`.

Write phi(z)=tanh(z)=2 sigmoid(2z)−1 and

    F(z;b,c)=sum_j c_j phi(z+b_j).

The bias and coefficient Jacobian columns are

    dF/db_j = c_j phi'(z+b_j),    dF/dc_j = phi(z+b_j).

The tangent ranks below concern functions over an open interval, and numerical Jacobians sampled at81 points in [−2,2]. They describe local first-order directions, not convergence rates or final generalization.

| Initialization | Trainable shape parameters | Bias-only rank | Full shape rank |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Fixed c=(1,−1,1), b=(0,0,0) | Three biases | 1 | 1 |
| Fixed c=(1,−1,1), b=(0,s,s), s≠0 | Three biases | 2 | 2 |
| Learned c=(1,0,0), b=(0,q1,q2), distinct centers | Three biases and three coefficients | 1 | 4 |

All three realize exactly phi(z), and therefore have the same shared-input derivative phi'(z). In the tiny fixture, adding the shared scalar input weight raises these ranks to2,3,5, respectively. Thus extra shape directions do not rescue a vanished upstream derivative while the forward map remains exactly unchanged; they can subsequently change that map.

#### Why the all-tied fixed initialization loses a degree of freedom

At b=(0,0,0), the bias columns are `(phi',−phi',phi')`, hence rank1.
More strongly, b1=b3 implies their per-example gradients are identical for every input and target. If they start equal with equal Adam states, learning rates and regularization, deterministic coordinatewise Adam preserves b1=b3 forever. This remains true under changing minibatches or evolving shared weights. The model therefore stays in the reduced family

    F(z)=2 phi(z+b_plus)−phi(z+b_minus),

which has only two independent bias coordinates, despite storing three. Positive and negative branches can separate, so this is not an identically frozen neuron; it is a symmetry constraint. Independent parameter perturbations/noise or unequal coordinate rules could break it but are different algorithms.

#### A function-preserving fixed-sign alternative

Set b=(0,s,s) for a nonzero center s. The second and third terms cancel exactly, so F=phi, but the bias columns become

    (phi'(z), −phi'(z+s), phi'(z+s)).

For tanh, phi'(z) and phi'(z+s) are linearly independent if s≠0. Their analytic continuations have distinct poles; equivalently, their ratio is nonconstant. Thus the rank is2, double the rank of the all-tied initialization with the SAME three trainable parameters. The canceling pair initially gets opposite gradients and can split, supplying a new first-order derivative-shaped feature. A perturbation obeys

    delta F(z)=delta b1*phi'(z)+(delta b3−delta b2)*phi'(z+s)+O(||delta b||^2).

The pair-average direction is initially null, as it must be: shifting both canceling terms equally leaves their cancellation intact. When the pair splits, the full three-bias tangent can become rank3. There is no claim that its optimization or test accuracy must beat either alternative.

For fixed alternating K=2R+1, keep one base term and R canceling pairs at distinct centers s_r. Then exact nesting remains, and the bias tangent has rank R+1 for tanh (provided centers are distinct), versus rank1 if everything is tied. This is ordinary function-preserving overparameterization and translated-derivative algebra; novelty has not been claimed or reviewed.

#### Learned zero-output terms activate through coefficients

With c=(1,0,0), the bias columns are `(phi'(z),0,0)`. The coefficient columns are `phi(z),phi(z+q1),phi(z+q2)`. With distinct q1,q2,0, the four nonzero functions are independent. To see this, use t=exp(2z): shifted tanh functions have simple poles at distinct negative t, while phi'(z) has a double pole at t=−1. A vanishing rational combination forces the double-pole coefficient and then each simple-pole coefficient to zero.

This gives full shape rank4, but uses six trainable shape parameters instead of three. At initialization extra bias gradients are zero. Extra coefficient gradients can be nonzero immediately and then make their bias gradients available. If the base coefficient is fixed at1, only the two extra coefficients train and the corresponding full shape rank is3. Rank comparisons must disclose this parameter-count distinction.

#### Conditioning and initialization recommendation

Distinct centers alone are insufficient: as s→0 the two derivative features become almost collinear; for |s| very large, the extra feature saturates over the observed projection range. The numerical probe includes s from0 to10 to expose both regimes.

A principled fixed-sign initialization experiment is therefore:

1. Preserve the base term at0.
2. Place a canceling pair at a distinct training-only projection quantile (with sign chosen because the argument is z+b).
3. Measure derivative-feature coverage and the smallest nonzero singular value of the activation Jacobian on a fixed training probe.
4. Compare with all-tied fixed signs and zero-coefficient learned profiles at matched optimizer/compute budgets.

This is a future ablation. Frozen image experiments remain unchanged; their all-tied fixed-K3 results should be interpreted as a particular symmetry-constrained initialization.

#### Checks

Analytic Jacobians using `sech^2` were compared against central differences of the independently written logistic forward expression. All three expected ranks, exact forward nesting and shared-input gradients passed. The fixed all-tied gradient equality and canceling-pair opposite gradients were verified for a nontrivial upstream signal. No optimization updates were run.

## Appendix 048: omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/ordered_band_agreement.md

Source: [omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/ordered_band_agreement.md](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/ordered_band_agreement.md). Original SHA256: `475e7fe15b8cdbab10b498337f580e35663ad3219bb62dbb2d8e2a8c87b0357d`.

This is the complete source note at compilation time. Its original experiment date, protocol, limitations and historical status apply; later corrections in the overview and subsequent audit notes take precedence. Heading levels, line endings, outer document spacing and source-relative Markdown links are normalized here; code and mathematical expressions are preserved.

### Ordered-band soft/hard agreement without a factor proportional to band count

This independently checks the local hardening bound in
`/tmp/band_segmentation.md` and sharpens a term-by-term binary alternating-band
bound. It is classical smoothing/partition algebra, not a novelty claim.

#### Ordered partition

Let \(\theta_1<\cdots<\theta_K\) and \(\beta>0\) be common to all terms. Define
\(s_j(x)=\sigma(\beta(x-\theta_j))\). The soft interval masses are

\[
q_0=1-s_1,\qquad q_r=s_r-s_{r+1}\ (1\le r<K),
\qquad q_K=s_K.
\]

Threshold ordering gives \(s_1>\cdots>s_K\); hence all masses are nonnegative,
and telescoping gives \(\sum_{r=0}^{K}q_r=1\). With no thresholds, define
\(q_0=1\). Equal thresholds can be merged; their intervening interval has
zero mass and no positive-margin interior.

Assign a deterministic class \(c_r\) to each hard interval and define

\[
p_c(x)=\sum_{\{r:c_r=c\}}q_r(x).
\]

This is a probability vector. Its equivalent sigmoid expansion is

\[
p(x)=e_{c_0}+
\sum_{j=1}^K(e_{c_j}-e_{c_{j-1}})
\sigma(\beta(x-\theta_j)).
\]

The vector coefficients are changes of one-hot labels, not arbitrary learned
readout vectors.

#### Local margin bound

Suppose \(x\in(\theta_r,\theta_{r+1})\) is in an interior interval. Let
\(d_L=x-\theta_r>0\), \(d_R=\theta_{r+1}-x>0\). Then

\[
q_r(x)=1-\sigma(-\beta d_L)-\sigma(-\beta d_R),
\]

so the assigned class has

\[
p_{c_r}(x)\ge1-\sigma(-\beta d_L)-\sigma(-\beta d_R).
\]

The exact local sufficient condition for unique argmax agreement is

\[
\sigma(-\beta d_L)+\sigma(-\beta d_R)<\tfrac12.
\]

If both distances are at least \(m>0\), the simpler sufficient condition is

\[
p_{c_r}(x)\ge1-\frac2{1+e^{\beta m}}>\tfrac12
\quad\text{when}\quad \beta m>\log3.
\]

The condition is sufficient, not necessary: other intervals may share the
same class and add probability to it. If adjacent intervals have the same
class, merging them can also improve the relevant distance.

For an exterior interval there is just one tail:

\[
p_{c_r}(x)\ge1-\sigma(-\beta d)>\tfrac12
\quad(d>0).
\]

At an exact boundary the positive-margin assumption fails. A unique argmax
agreement guarantee cannot be inferred from this theorem. A constant
one-interval classifier agrees identically.

#### Binary alternating bands and the improved error bound

For arbitrary binary interval labels \(y_r\in\{0,1\}\), let \(h(x)=y_r\) in
interval \(r\), and \(p(x)=\sum_r y_rq_r(x)\). Then

\[
|p(x)-h(x)|\le1-q_r(x)
\le\frac2{1+e^{\beta m}}
\]

for an interior point with the stated margin. The exterior version has
one tail. In particular, this applies to a valid fixed-alternating hard unit
starting at zero, whose successive interval labels are \(0,1,0,1,\ldots\).
It replaces the loose triangle-inequality estimate
\(K/(1+e^{\beta m})\) by a bound involving only the two adjacent boundaries.

An independent interpretation makes the cancellation explicit. If
\(\varepsilon\) is centered logistic noise with CDF \(\sigma(\beta u)\), then

\[
q_r(x)=\Pr[x+\varepsilon\text{ lies in interval }r],
\qquad p(x)=\mathbb E[h(x+\varepsilon)].
\]

Changing the output label requires leaving the current interval. The two
tail probabilities bound that event regardless of how many more cuts exist.
Thus there is no accumulation of \(K\) independent boundary errors.

The factor two is sharp as a universal local bound: use only two cuts
\(-m,+m\), assign the middle interval label one and both exterior intervals
label zero, and evaluate at \(x=0\). Then

\[
p(0)=1-\frac2{1+e^{\beta m}}.
\]

At \(e^{\beta m}=3\), this gives exactly a 1/2 tie; below three it can give
the wrong hard binary decision. For multiclass probabilities,
\(\|p-e_{c_r}\|_1=2(1-p_{c_r})\), so the corresponding L1 bound is four tails
in the equal-margin notation, while total-variation error is at most two.

#### What the bound does and does not cover

- It proves agreement with the **fitted hard band classifier**, including
  that classifier's errors. It does not establish ground-truth correctness.
- Cuts must be ordered and share a positive temperature. Different
  temperatures can make adjacent sigmoids cross and produce negative
  putative interval masses.
- Arbitrary learned coefficients/offsets need not produce probabilities or
  soften a valid binary indicator. The bound cannot be transferred to them
  solely because they use multiple biases.
- Distances are scalar score margins. For \(x=w^\top X+b\), conversion to
  Euclidean input-space margins divides distances by \(\|w\|_2\).
- The theorem is in real arithmetic. Floating-point model evaluation and
  upstream score uncertainty require their own rounding/enclosure analysis.
  These tests do not make the soft readout part of the rational DP certificate.
- Logistic convolution is an interpretation of the specified smooth
  expectation; it does not differentiate a discontinuous hard predicate.

#### Independent checks

`/tmp/ordered_band_agreement.py` uses exact `Fraction` arithmetic with rational
\(t=e^{\beta x}\), \(a_j=e^{\beta\theta_j}\). Then
\(s_j=t/(t+a_j)\), so all tested masses and error bounds are exact.
It checks sharp interior cases with rational \(e^{\beta m}\), exterior and
boundary cases, 96 seeded small ordered partitions, arbitrary repeated class
assignments, alternating binary labels, telescoping compilation, constant
classifiers, and a differing-temperature counterexample. The retained JSON
includes source/proof fingerprints. No learning or performance claim follows.

## Appendix 049: omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/pair_descent_theorem.md

Source: [omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/pair_descent_theorem.md](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/pair_descent_theorem.md). Original SHA256: `f077bf277e5254f1e7395677c090fc3f4669ef14354fbf22e2e1100d43362f1e`.

This is the complete source note at compilation time. Its original experiment date, protocol, limitations and historical status apply; later corrections in the overview and subsequent audit notes take precedence. Heading levels, line endings, outer document spacing and source-relative Markdown links are normalized here; code and mathematical expressions are preserved.

### Local descent from an exactly canceling sigmoid pair

Independent mathematical verification, 20 October2026. No training, frozen-package changes or performance claims. Complete rational checks: `/tmp/pair_descent_theorem.py`; retained results: `/tmp/pair_descent_theorem.json`.

#### Statement and assumptions

Let sigma_beta(u)=1/(1+exp(−beta*u)), beta>0. A differentiable empirical loss depends on scalar values f_l at fixed projected scores z_l. Aggregate the value gradients at each distinct score:

    r_i = sum_{l:z_l=z_i} dLoss/df_l.

Let z_1,...,z_N be distinct, and assume r is not the zero vector. Zero entries can be removed when counting N. Add the branch

    p_delta(z)=c[sigma_beta(z+s+delta)−sigma_beta(z+s−delta)], c≠0.

At delta=0 this is identically zero, for every real z. Its loss derivative is

    D(s) := (d/delta) Loss(f+p_delta)|delta=0
          = 2c sum_i r_i sigma_beta'(z_i+s).

There exists a center s with D(s)≠0. Therefore delta=−eta*sign(D(s)) strictly decreases this empirical loss for all sufficiently small eta>0. This follows directly from differentiability, without a convergence or finite-step-size claim.

For an internal activation, r_i must be the actual upstream feature gradient. If that aggregated gradient is zero, the conclusion does not apply. Signed delta must be feasible; fixed coefficient signs plus an ordered/nonnegative-band constraint can exclude the needed direction. The theorem concerns the data loss or an objective whose architecture insertion and local regularizer derivative are accounted for. Adding nonzero ±c copies generally increases parameter-count/L1 penalties even though the forward function is unchanged.

#### Elementary rational proof: any 2N−1 centers suffice

Set a_i=exp(−beta*z_i)>0 and t=exp(beta*s)>0. The a_i are distinct. Then

    G(t) = sum_i r_i beta*a_i*t/(t+a_i)^2,
    D(s)=2c G(exp(beta*s)).

Multiply by the common denominator and divide by beta*t:

    Q(t)=sum_i r_i a_i product_{k≠i}(t+a_k)^2.

Its degree is at most2N−2. It is not identically zero, since

    Q(−a_j)=r_j*a_j*product_{k≠j}(a_k−a_j)^2,

which is nonzero whenever r_j≠0. Thus G has at most2N−2 positive zeros. Any2N−1 distinct finite centers include a nonzero derivative witness. This proves the original proposed statement without additional hypotheses beyond those above.

#### Stronger elementary data-centered result: N candidates suffice

Choose s_j=−z_j. Define

    K_ji=sigma_beta'(z_i−z_j)
        =beta*a_i*a_j/(a_i+a_j)^2.

The loss derivatives at these N centers are2c*K*r. The matrix K is strictly positive definite. Indeed, for a nonzero vector v,

    v^T K v = beta*integral_0^infinity t[sum_i v_i*a_i*exp(−a_i*t)]^2 dt >0.

The integral representation uses integral_0^infinity t*exp(−(a_i+a_j)t)dt=(a_i+a_j)^−2. To prove strictness, a zero integral would force the continuous exponential sum to vanish identically. Order the distinct a_i increasingly, multiply by exp(a_1*t), and let t→infinity to obtain v_1*a_1=0; repeat inductively to show every v_i=0, a contradiction.

Consequently K*r≠0, and at least one of the N data-centered candidates is a strict local descent witness. Quantitatively,

    max_j |D(s_j)| >= 2|c| lambda_min(K) ||r||_2 / sqrt(N).

There is no data-independent positive lower bound on lambda_min. Nevertheless a computable certified substitute is

    alpha = 1 / ||K^−1||_infinity <= lambda_min(K),

because K^−1 is symmetric and its spectral norm is at most its maximum absolute row sum. If a_i and beta are rational, alpha and the squared lower bound can be checked with exact rational arithmetic. The script does so, in addition to exact positive LDL pivots and reconstruction.

Conditioning nuance: near-coincident scores make K nearly singular. Absolute score shifts do not change K, and well-separated scores make its off-diagonal entries small relative to its beta/4 diagonal; they improve its conditioning. Saturated off-data centers can give tiny derivatives, but the data-centered construction places one derivative peak on each score and avoids that particular problem. Arithmetic underflow/rounding and dense score spacing still matter in an implementation.

Computing all N candidates by a dense matrix costs O(N²); this existence theorem does not establish a faster optimizer. A small quantile subset is an approximation and does not inherit the N-candidate guarantee automatically.

#### Further classical refinement: any N distinct centers suffice

For arbitrary distinct centers, t_j=exp(beta*s_j)>0. The evaluation matrix is

    B_ji=beta*t_j*a_i/(t_j+a_i)^2.

Positive diagonal scalings reduce its invertibility to the squared Cauchy matrix D_ji=(t_j+a_i)^−2. By the classical Borchardt identity,

    det D = det C * per C,   C_ji=(t_j+a_i)^−1.

Cauchy's determinant formula makes det C nonzero for distinct t_j and distinct a_i, while every entry of C is positive, so per C>0. Hence B is invertible. Every N distinct centers contain a nonzero witness for every nonzero r. The explicit data-centered construction above is particularly convenient because it yields a symmetric positive-definite matrix and the quantitative bound.

The arbitrary-N identity is classical; see [Chavez et al., Inductive Proof of Borchardt's Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.05886), or the displayed plus-form in [Ishikawa, Kawamuko and Okada, A Pfaffian–Hafnian analogue of Borchardt's identity, EJC2005](https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/download/v12i1n9/pdf/). The script independently verifies determinant/permanent equality with exact permutation sums in four tiny rational fixtures.

The number N is worst-case sharp for a guarantee based on fixed candidate centers: fewer than N rows give an evaluation matrix with a nontrivial null vector r. A concrete one-center failure is a=(1,4), r=(16,−25): G(1)=0 but G(2)=−2.

#### What fails outside the assumptions

- Opposing gradients on identical projections can cancel: a=(1,1), r=(1,−1) gives G=0 at every center. Aggregate tied scores first.
- If r_i>0 and c>0, D(s)>0 for every center. Restricting delta≥0 forbids descent; negative delta or a coefficient sign change is needed.
- If the upstream derivative is zero, adding a differentiable branch through that dead downstream path does not create a nonzero r.
- Function preservation does not preserve arbitrary parameter regularizers or storage cost.
- A nonzero derivative may be extremely small. There is no uniform practical step size, convergence rate, minibatch stability, test-risk improvement, or escape guarantee for every stationary deep network.
- Repeatedly adding terms can fit noise. This lemma provides a local training-loss mechanism; validation, complexity control and matched-resource comparisons remain necessary.

#### Targeted prior-art comparison

The broad mechanism of function-preserving growth guided by gradient information already exists. [GradMax (Evci et al., ICLR2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.05125) chooses new-unit initialization to increase gradient signal without changing the learned function. [Splitting Steepest Descent (Liu, Wu and Wang2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02366) develops functional descent by neuron splitting; [Signed Neural Splitting (Wu et al.2020/2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.10392) specifically uses positive and negative copies to address splitting stability. These are direct comparisons for any proposed architectural-growth claim.

Selecting a translated derivative with nonzero residual correlation is also a dictionary/functional-gradient argument. The result here is a precise restricted-family corollary: bias-only logistic pairs, exact initial cancellation, explicit finite candidate count, and a positive-definite-kernel certificate. The proof is complete under its assumptions, but novelty is unestablished; these classical identities and related growth methods prevent calling the general mechanism a new invention.

#### Retained checks

Four fixtures with N=1,2,3,5 use exact Fraction arithmetic for the polynomial identity, pole evaluations, witness values, Borchardt determinant/permanent identity, positive-definite LDL decomposition, matrix inverse and certified gradient lower bound. Independent floating logistic finite differences match the rational derivatives. An analytic squared loss is evaluated before and after a single sufficiently small signed perturbation to illustrate strict decrease; no optimizer or training loop runs. Tied-score cancellation and a bad fixed candidate are checked explicitly. Exact2x2 eigenvalues demonstrate poor conditioning for nearly equal scores and good conditioning for widely separated scores.

All checks passed in approximately0.023 seconds of computation. The analytical proof, not the numerical fixtures, supplies the general guarantee.

#### Additional independent audit clarifications

The composite objective must be differentiable with respect to the inserted activation values; a downstream ReLU kink is not covered just because the final loss is smooth. Exact rational checking of the complete squared gradient bound also requires rational residual gradients and coefficient c. Generic floating scores yield transcendental transformed coordinates a_i, so real-model certificates require interval enclosures. Any output-range constraint must allow the selected split; a signed pair need not remain in [0,1].

## Appendix 050: omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/pair_growth_search.md

Source: [omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/pair_growth_search.md](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/pair_growth_search.md). Original SHA256: `a3509df46d2354833337828be3cb68934088cc0acbf2e65eefc94622f38b36b5`.

This is the complete source note at compilation time. Its original experiment date, protocol, limitations and historical status apply; later corrections in the overview and subsequent audit notes take precedence. Heading levels, line endings, outer document spacing and source-relative Markdown links are normalized here; code and mathematical expressions are preserved.

### Residual-guided canceling-pair growth proposal

Research-only implementation: `/tmp/pair_growth_search.py`. Independently checked fixtures and source fingerprint: `/tmp/pair_growth_search.json`. Mathematical basis: `/tmp/pair_descent_theorem.md`. No frozen image-package changes or training runs were made.

#### API

```python
result = propose_pair_growth(
    scores, baseline_predictions, loss_and_grad,
    beta=1.0,
    coefficient=1.0,
    candidate_shifts=None,  # all distinct data-centered shifts -z_i
    initial_split=0.1,
    max_backtracks=24,
    insertion_cost=0.0,
    split_l2=0.0,
    score_chunk=4096,
    candidate_chunk=32,
)
```

`loss_and_grad(predictions)` returns a finite scalar empirical loss and its correct gradient with respect to that prediction vector. The callback receives a protected copy and must be deterministic for reproducible search. The API returns a proposal; it never changes a model or its optimizer.

For a successful result, the proposed added function is

    p(z)=c[sigma_beta(z+s+delta)−sigma_beta(z+s−delta)].

The result includes s, delta, beta, c and finite two biases/coefficients. In real arithmetic the two parameterizations are equivalent; rounding may change their functions. `pair_values` evaluates the canonical center/split representation. Delta0 returns literal zeros, preserving the baseline exactly. Moderate nonzero splits use the stable identity

    sigma(u+d)−sigma(u−d)=sinh(d)/(cosh(u)+cosh(d))

in log form, reducing cancellation near zero without overflowing hyperbolic functions. For large splits (`abs(beta*delta)>32`), separate branch arguments are evaluated instead. This retains the 1/2 contribution when, for example, u=d=10^20: the pair is sigma(2×10^20)−sigma(0)=1/2, whereas subtracting enormous log quantities loses that correction. When both arguments are positive the evaluator subtracts complementary tail sigmoids to retain small differences. Unsupported overflowing intermediate quantities are rejected.

Every proposed export is independently evaluated from its actual rounded `bias_plus` and `bias_minus` on all observed scores. Identical rounded biases from a nonzero split are rejected. Other mismatches exceeding `export_atol + export_rtol*max(abs(canonical_pair))` are also rejected (defaults 10^-12 and 10^-10). The actual export's predictions pay the objective and Armijo checks. The result labels its parameterization `two_bias_export_checked_on_observed_scores`; this numerical check does not establish off-sample equality of the representations or a global functional-error bound.

#### Search procedure and theorem link

1. Evaluate the baseline loss and its prediction gradients.
2. Aggregate gradients at exactly identical projected scores.
3. For each candidate center, compute

       D(s)=2c sum_i r_i sigma_beta'(z_i+s).

4. Select the largest absolute derivative deterministically.
5. Search signed splits opposite that derivative, verify the rounded bias export, and accept only its actually evaluated total empirical objective satisfying strict Armijo decrease and the recorded numerical tolerance.

With distinct scores and nonzero aggregated gradients, N data-centered candidates contain a nonzero derivative witness in exact arithmetic. This is the positive-definite-kernel result proved in the linked theorem. Finite floating arithmetic, a gradient tolerance, or a bounded backtracking budget can still leave the proposal inconclusive. An explicit subset of candidate centers may miss a witness altogether.

Correlations are computed in blocks; no dense N×M matrix is allocated. Arithmetic cost is O(NM), and workspace is O(score_chunk*candidate_chunk+N+M). The output reports matrix entries and largest block size. Choosing all N centers costs O(N²) arithmetic even though memory is bounded. No speedup claim follows.

#### Results and refusal semantics

- `DESCENT_FOUND`: a finite tested proposal decreases the empirical objective beyond tolerance and satisfies Armijo. The accepted objective includes `insertion_cost + split_l2*delta²`.
- `NO_FIRST_ORDER_SIGNAL`: aggregated gradients are exactly zero in the performed float64 arithmetic. This is not a certified global or local optimum.
- `INCONCLUSIVE`: examples include insufficient candidate coverage, numerical signal below tolerance, exhausted backtracking, regularization cost, nonfinite trial evaluations, or an unrepresentable rounded bias export.
- `INVALID_INPUT`: malformed arrays/hyperparameters or an invalid baseline loss/gradient callback.

Nonfinite inputs, derived quantities and callback values cannot produce an accepted proposal. A wrong supplied gradient can propose the wrong direction; actual objective checks prevent acceptance unless the evaluated objective really decreases, but the API cannot establish that an arbitrary callback's derivative is mathematically correct.

Parameter regularization requires explicit care. Adding a ±c pair preserves outputs but may increase parameter penalties. The API compares to the ORIGINAL baseline objective and includes the specified insertion cost; a pair that decreases data loss but fails to pay for its regularization is rejected. Callers must supply all relevant extra costs.

#### Independent fixtures

Twenty-one tiny CPU tests passed:

- Full-center descent with both positive and negative c.
- A large initial split reduced by successful backtracking.
- A deliberately bad single center and a saturated off-data center.
- Empty candidates and exact cancellation of gradients on tied scores.
- A regularization cost that blocks accepting a data-loss improvement.
- Nonfinite scores/gradients/trial losses/derived derivatives and invalid hyperparameters.
- A deliberately inconsistent gradient callback that fails actual-loss acceptance.
- Independent dense `beta/(2+2cosh(...))` correlations versus bounded blocks.
- Stable pair values versus direct logistic differences and independent derivative formulas.
- Large equal u,d, including 10^20 and 10^300, with independently known half-height values; positive-tail and 10^-20 split regressions.
- An overflowing derived bias rejected before evaluating loss, followed by successful backtracking to finite export parameters.
- Nonzero splits whose derived biases collapse to the same float.
- Noncollapsed but materially distorted gaps at large offsets, checked against the independent exported evaluator.

The checks take about 0.025 seconds of numerical computation. They evaluate simple analytic losses; there is no optimizer, fitted model, dataset or GPU job. The large-argument and export checks correct edge defects found during independent code audit; the earlier 17-test result did not cover them.

#### Quantitative conditioning refinement

Let ordered distinct projected scores have minimum spacing d>0. For the data-centered matrix K,

    K_ii=beta/4,
    K_ij=beta/[4cosh²(beta(z_i−z_j)/2)] <= beta exp(−beta|z_i−z_j|).

At most one score per index-distance k lies on each side, so each off-diagonal row sum is bounded by

    2 beta sum_{k>=1} exp(−beta*k*d)
    =2 beta/(exp(beta*d)−1).

If beta*d≥log17, this is at most beta/8. Gershgorin therefore gives

    beta/8 <= lambda_min(K) <= lambda_max(K) <= 3beta/8,
    condition_number_2(K) <= 3.

This is a supported conditioning corollary for the local dictionary. Increasing temperature to resolve small spacing may require beta proportional to1/d, increase sensitivity and encourage fitting noise. It is not a global optimizer prescription or a generalization guarantee. The API does not automatically choose temperature using this rule.

Histogram approximation was omitted: explicit subsets and chunked exact float64 correlations suffice for this bounded prototype. A future histogram method must carry its own approximation error and cannot inherit the full-candidate witness guarantee without checking that error.

#### Interpretation

This is a concrete adaptive-bias growth mechanism linked to a complete local-descent argument. Function-preserving gradient-guided growth and signed splitting have close prior art (GradMax and Signed Neural Splitting, cited in the theorem memo). Mathematical novelty, practical performance, validation improvement and generalization remain unestablished. A downstream study should compare this proposal against zero-coefficient growth and conventional neuron growth at matched computation/storage, retaining validation rollback.

## Appendix 051: omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/profile_crossing_bound.md

Source: [omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/profile_crossing_bound.md](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/profile_crossing_bound.md). Original SHA256: `d8b22012a647011c333c7a809893e04cdb7829ae9fb07ab26483095e44296aaa`.

This is the complete source note at compilation time. Its original experiment date, protocol, limitations and historical status apply; later corrections in the overview and subsequent audit notes take precedence. Heading levels, line endings, outer document spacing and source-relative Markdown links are normalized here; code and mathematical expressions are preserved.

### Oscillation and classification budget of a common-temperature sigmoid profile

Read-only mathematical follow-up; no model changes, training, or numerical jobs.

Let

\[
p(z)=d+\sum_{j=1}^{K}c_j\sigma(\beta(z+b_j)),\qquad
\sigma(s)=\frac1{1+e^{-s}},
\]

where all parameters are finite and real and \(\beta>0\) is common to every term.
Combine terms with identical biases by adding their coefficients, then remove
zero combined coefficients. Write \(m\le K\) for the remaining number. These
conditions matter: independently varying slopes fall outside this result.

#### Threshold roots

Set \(t=e^{\beta z}>0\), \(a_j=e^{-\beta b_j}>0\). Distinct remaining biases give
distinct \(a_j\), and

\[
p(z)-\tau=(d-\tau)+\sum_{j=1}^{m}c_j\frac{t}{t+a_j}
          =\frac{N(t)}{D(t)},
\qquad D(t)=\prod_{j=1}^{m}(t+a_j)>0.
\]

The numerator

\[
N(t)=(d-\tau)D(t)+
\sum_{j=1}^{m}c_j t\prod_{k\ne j}(t+a_k)
\]

has degree at most \(m\). Therefore either \(p\equiv\tau\), or \(p(z)=\tau\)
has at most \(m\) distinct real solutions. This counts tangencies as roots;
the number of actual sign crossings may be smaller.

With the merged nonzero-coefficient convention, \(m>0\) rules out
\(p\equiv\tau\): its rational partial fraction at \(-a_j\) has nonzero residue
\(-c_j a_j\). The identically-threshold case is exactly the constant profile
with \(m=0,d=\tau\).

#### Stationary points

Differentiating gives

\[
\frac{p'(z)}{\beta t}
 =\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{c_j a_j}{(t+a_j)^2}.
\]

Suppose a nonconstant profile had \(m\) distinct stationary points, corresponding
to distinct positive \(t_1,\ldots,t_m\). Then the nonzero vector
\((c_j a_j)_{j=1}^{m}\) would belong to the nullspace of

\[
B_{ij}=\frac1{(t_i+a_j)^2}.
\]

This matrix is invertible. Borchardt's identity gives

\[
\det B=
\det\left[\frac1{t_i+a_j}\right]\,
\operatorname{per}\left[\frac1{t_i+a_j}\right].
\]

The permanent is strictly positive because all matrix entries are positive.
The Cauchy determinant is nonzero for distinct \(t_i\) and distinct \(a_j\):

\[
\det\left[\frac1{t_i+a_j}\right]
=\frac{\prod_{i<k}(t_k-t_i)\prod_{j<\ell}(a_\ell-a_j)}
       {\prod_{i,j}(t_i+a_j)}
\]

after adopting the displayed ordering. Contradiction. Consequently a
nonconstant profile has at most \(m-1\) **distinct stationary points**.
This statement excludes constant profiles, whose derivative vanishes
everywhere. It is a statement about distinct zeros, not their multiplicities.

Borchardt's identity and the Cauchy determinant are classical; a modern
primary-source proof is [Chavez et al., *Inductive Proof of Borchardt's
Theorem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.05886). The profile result follows from
this established algebra; novelty has not been established.

#### Both bounds are tight

Fix any distinct positive \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) and choose any distinct positive
roots \(r_1,\ldots,r_m\). Let

\[
D(t)=\prod_j(t+a_j),\qquad N(t)=A\prod_i(t-r_i),\quad A\ne0.
\]

The rational function \(N/D\) has exactly those \(m\) simple positive roots.
It is realized by the profile using

\[
c_j=-\frac{N(-a_j)}{a_j D'(-a_j)},\qquad
d-\tau=\frac{N(0)}{D(0)}.
\]

To verify the formula, the residues of both expressions at \(-a_j\) agree,
and their values at \(t=0\) agree. Their difference has no poles, is bounded
at infinity, and vanishes at zero, so it is identically zero.
All \(c_j\) are nonzero because each \(r_i>0\).

The resulting \(p-\tau\) has exactly \(m\) simple threshold crossings.
Rolle's theorem supplies at least \(m-1\) distinct stationary points between
them, while the previous bound permits at most \(m-1\). Thus both bounds
are attained by the same construction.

For example, \(a_1=1,a_2=2\), \(\tau=0\), and
\(N(t)=(t-1)(t-2)\) give

\[
p(z)=1-6\frac{t}{t+1}+6\frac{t}{t+2},\qquad t=e^{\beta z}.
\]

It has two crossings at \(t=1,2\) and one stationary point at \(t=\sqrt2\).
This is an analytic check, with no numerical fitting.

#### Exact strict-label capacity on a fixed projection ordering

Consider \(N\) distinct ordered scores \(z_1<\cdots<z_N\), and require strict
classification: no fitted score may equal the threshold.
A profile with at most \(K\) terms can realize only label sequences with at
most \(K\) transitions, by the intermediate value theorem and the root bound.

Conversely, any label sequence with \(q\le K\) transitions is realizable.
Place a positive root \(r_i\) between the transformed scores at each
transition, use the degree-\(q\) construction above, and choose the sign of
\(A\) to match the first label. A constant realizes \(q=0\); unused terms
may receive coefficient zero. This argument requires unrestricted real
coefficients and a freely chosen offset.

Therefore the exact number of strict binary labelings on this fixed order is

\[
2\sum_{q=0}^{\min(K,N-1)}\binom{N-1}{q}.
\]

This is not a closed-form count of all Boolean threshold functions:
changing the projection changes the score order, and different orders may
realize overlapping labelings. Tied scores must first be merged; they cannot
receive different labels from a scalar profile. Samples exactly on the
threshold are deliberately excluded from this strict-classification count.

##### Difference from the fixed-alternating, far-left-zero hard unit

For an ordered hard-threshold unit with at most \(K\) fixed alternating
coefficients \(+1,-1,+1,\ldots\), the response starts at zero on the far left.
A finite sample sequence starting at one spends one threshold before its first
sample. Thus a sequence with \(q\) internal transitions requires
\(q+y_1\) thresholds, where \(y_1\in\{0,1\}\) is its first label. The count is

\[
\sum_{q=0}^{K}\binom{N-1}{q}
+\sum_{q=0}^{K-1}\binom{N-1}{q}
=\sum_{q=0}^{\min(K,N)}\binom{N}{q},
\]

using the convention that binomial coefficients outside their range vanish.
The learned-offset profile above has both starting labels available without
spending a sigmoid term; hence its different count.

This hard-unit count is not automatically an achievability result for
fixed-sign finite-temperature sigmoid profiles on fixed, poorly separated
scores. Such units require a separate smoothing/separation argument.
The free-coefficient rational construction does apply at any fixed
\(\beta>0\), but its coefficients can become poorly conditioned.

#### Implications and limits

- For a ridge field \(p(v^\top x)\) with \(v\ne0\), each isolated threshold
  root corresponds to a parallel hyperplane. At most \(K\) such roots occur.
  If \(v=0\), the field is constant.
- A target with \(q\) alternating above/below-threshold observations along
  a projection requires at least \(q-1\) effective terms to fit those strict
  labels. Arbitrary learned coefficients do not evade this oscillation budget.
- Rich profiles can replace repeated projections that differ mainly through
  one-dimensional response shape. They do not restore information discarded
  by the chosen projection, and their finite oscillation budget still limits
  how much compositional depth they can replace.
- The constructive result may require large, canceling coefficients. It gives
  representation capacity, not conditioning, stable training, margins,
  generalization, or computational efficiency.
- A sum over different projection directions, independently learned slopes,
  and multiclass comparisons between different dictionaries require separate
  accounting. They cannot inherit the scalar \(K\)-root bound unchanged.

#### Independent exact checks

`/tmp/profile_crossing_bound.py` uses only Python's standard library and
`fractions.Fraction`. It checks constructive partial fractions at
\(m=1,2,3,5\) by polynomial coefficients and independent rational evaluations;
checks all chosen roots and alternating signs between them; checks the
Borchardt/Cauchy identities at rational positive arguments; enumerates both
fixed-order labeling counts on small problems; constructs every eligible
six-score, three-term strict labeling; and checks merged-bias cancellation
and incompatible tied labels. Results and source fingerprints are retained in
`/tmp/profile_crossing_bound.json`. Finite fixtures corroborate the algebra;
the proof above supplies the universal statement. No training is involved.

## Appendix 052: omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/profile_crossing_independent_review.md

Source: [omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/profile_crossing_independent_review.md](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/profile_crossing_independent_review.md). Original SHA256: `da5a3bf8f0f1d87af5b043d3c85c613f6a0ec078c101c78ca6bd945260062ab2`.

This is the complete source note at compilation time. Its original experiment date, protocol, limitations and historical status apply; later corrections in the overview and subsequent audit notes take precedence. Heading levels, line endings, outer document spacing and source-relative Markdown links are normalized here; code and mathematical expressions are preserved.

### Independent review: crossing budget and depth replacement

Read-only review of `/tmp/profile_crossing_bound.md`, 20 October 2026. No training, timing jobs or source edits were performed.

#### Verdict

The threshold-root bound, stationary-point bound, constructive sharpness and exact fixed-order count are sound under the stated common-temperature, shared-projection and free-coefficient assumptions. The transfer to the classical parallel-threshold counting bound is also valid for **strict binary labels**. There is one wording error to fix: the implications bullet says “q alternating ... observations ... requires at least q ... terms.” If q counts observations, the bound is q−1 terms. The q-term bound is correct when q counts transitions.

#### Checks of the stated proof

1. With t=exp(beta*z), a_j=exp(−beta*b_j), the denominator D(t) is strictly positive on t>0 and the numerator has degree at most m. Thus the stated threshold-root bound holds. After merging equal biases, nonzero c_j yield nonzero residues −c_j*a_j, so a nonconstant representation cannot become identically threshold-valued by cancellation across distinct biases.
2. The stationary-point evaluation matrix has entries (t_i+a_j)^−2. Borchardt gives its determinant as a nonzero Cauchy determinant times a strictly positive permanent. Therefore a nonzero coefficient vector cannot have m distinct derivative zeros. This proves at most m−1 distinct stationary points. It does not require any coefficient sign restriction. The document correctly excludes constant profiles and makes no unsupported multiplicity assertion.
3. The residue formula c_j=−N(−a_j)/(a_j D'(−a_j)) and d−tau=N(0)/D(0) is correct. Equal residues and the value at zero identify the bounded rational functions. Positive target roots and negative poles cannot coincide, so every constructed coefficient is nonzero. The resulting m simple crossings imply m−1 stationary points by Rolle, achieving both bounds.
4. The two-term example is correct: p=1−6t/(t+1)+6t/(t+2) has roots 1 and 2, and its sole stationary point is sqrt(2).
5. For N>=1 ordered distinct scores and at most K terms, strict labels have at most K internal transitions. Conversely the constructive rational profile realizes any choice of q<=K transition gaps, with either first label. Therefore the exact count is 2*sum_{q=0}^{min(K,N−1)} binom(N−1,q). Constants cover q=0. The freely chosen offset is essential to the proof as written; do not transfer this count to the far-left-zero fixed-sign unit.
6. The hard fixed-alternating count sum_{q=0}^{min(K,N)} binom(N,q) is correct, with binomial coefficients outside range treated as zero. The distinction between a hard-unit count and finite-temperature fixed-sign realizability on fixed scores is appropriately explicit.

#### Transfer to the Boolean-universality lower bound

For any scalar profile p(w^T x) with K common-temperature sigmoid terms and an offset, consider its strict binary labels on the Boolean cube. If w=0 or p is constant, it is a constant labeling. Otherwise, merge tied projected scores; opposite labels on the same score are impossible. Arrange the distinct scores in order. Each label transition requires a distinct root of p−tau in the corresponding open gap, so there are at most K transitions.

Place hard parallel thresholds at those transition roots or anywhere in their gaps and choose the appropriate initial class label. This gives a free-polarity multilevel threshold classifier with at most K planes that agrees on every cube vertex. Thus the learned-coefficient profile class, restricted to strict binary labels, is a subclass of the hard parallel-threshold class used in Anthony's growth bound. This subset argument permits beta, w, biases, coefficients and offset to depend arbitrarily on the target labeling; it requires only that each realized profile use a common positive beta and a single shared projection.

Consequently, for n,K>=1, N=2^n and r=n+K−1,

    # realizable strict cube labelings
      <= 2 sum_{i=0}^r binom(KN,i)
      <= 2 (eKN/r)^r
      <= 2^(1+r(n+log2(e))).

Covering all 2^N Boolean functions requires

    K >= ceil((2^n−1)/(n+log2(e)) − n + 1).

This is a conservative Omega(2^n/n) necessary condition, not an exact minimum. It legitimately covers the common-temperature learned-coefficient sigmoid profile described here. Independent per-term slopes, sums over different projection directions, vector-valued classifiers with different dictionaries, or non-strict labels exactly on roots require separate accounting.

Strictness is useful: tangencies exactly at sampled scores can produce isolated threshold-equality labels under a >= convention. The current transition proof deliberately avoids treating such boundary labels as robust classification. There is no need to resolve that different convention to state this theorem.

#### A concise depth-replacement obstruction

Let x(t)=x_0+t*u be an affine line, with t_1<...<t_M. Suppose a scalar teacher F has alternating strict labels with positive output margin gamma:

    sign(F(x(t_i))−tau) alternates with i,
    |F(x(t_i))−tau| >= gamma > 0.

Consider a replacement G(x)=p(v^T x), where p is one common-temperature profile with K effective terms.

If v^T u=0, G is constant on that line and cannot match the alternating labels when M>=2. If v^T u!=0, the projected scores are strictly monotone in t, possibly in reverse order. A replacement with

    max_i |G(x(t_i))−F(x(t_i))| < gamma

must match all teacher labels strictly. The root bound then forces

    K >= M−1.

Equivalently, when K<M−1, every such replacement has maximum error at least gamma on those points. Its mean squared error on the M equally weighted points is at least gamma^2/M. This is a necessary condition, not a sufficient construction, and concerns error relative to this particular teacher; it does not prove the teacher is Bayes-optimal or needed for the original task.

The stronger elementary counting version is available if useful: a binary sequence with at most K transitions differs from a length-M alternating sequence at least ceil((M−1−K)/2) times when K<M−1, because changing one label can eliminate at most two transitions. Thus the empirical squared-error lower bound can be multiplied by this integer, provided non-strict/equality cases are handled consistently. The simpler one-error bound above avoids that extra convention.

If a depth-L teacher supplies M=2^L such margin-separated alternating observations on an affine line, the single-profile replacement needs at least 2^L−1 effective terms at error below gamma. The existence and margin of that teacher must be separately proved; this conditional statement does not establish that every deep network has exponential oscillation.

#### Why sums over different directions need a different bound

For G(x)=d+sum_g p_g(v_g^T x), restriction to the line yields sigmoid slopes beta_g*(v_g^T u), which can differ across groups. A common beta before taking projections does not make those line slopes equal. Therefore the single-profile K-root bound cannot be assigned to the total term count automatically.

A useful special case does reduce: if all nonzero effective line slopes have the same magnitude, negative slopes can be flipped using sigmoid(−a)=1−sigmoid(a), with their constants absorbed into d. The resulting restriction is a single common-slope profile, so the bound uses the total number of distinct effective shifted terms. Zero slopes contribute constants.

For unrestricted effective slopes, a much looser general line bound can be derived if needed. A scalar sum of H sigmoid terms with arbitrary finite real slopes has, after multiplication by its positive product denominator, an exponential polynomial with at most 2^H distinct exponential rates. A nonzero exponential polynomial with J distinct real rates has at most J−1 distinct real zeros (factor out the smallest exponential, differentiate, and use induction and Rolle). Hence at most 2^H−1 crossings follows unless the scalar function is identically threshold-valued. This bound is deliberately loose; it does not show that 2^H−1 crossings are attainable or that different-direction sums efficiently represent the teacher. It explains why the sharp linear K obstruction must remain scoped to one common-slope profile.

#### Scope and novelty

These are consequences of classical rational-function, Cauchy/Borchardt, growth-function and Rolle arguments. The proofs support a precise structural limitation and a conditional depth-replacement certificate. They do not by themselves establish a new learning algorithm, a general depth theorem, conditioning guarantees or competitive performance.

## Appendix 053: omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/profile_math_review.md

Source: [omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/profile_math_review.md](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/profile_math_review.md). Original SHA256: `7ea898e1420341df05ed9db088848c3e3799fec18fbd24e3d624af513d30e3c8`.

This is the complete source note at compilation time. Its original experiment date, protocol, limitations and historical status apply; later corrections in the overview and subsequent audit notes take precedence. Heading levels, line endings, outer document spacing and source-relative Markdown links are normalized here; code and mathematical expressions are preserved.

### Read-only mathematical audit: multi-bias activation research

No source, paper, API or artifact was modified. This audit concerns the actual model family, not a claim that all activation variants are equivalent. Paths/lines were read on 20 October 2026.

#### 1. What the existing paper and implementation actually contain

- `multi_bias/paper/main.tex:395–411` defines `sum s_k sigma(z+b_k)` and explicitly distinguishes fixed alternating signs from learned real coefficients. The ReLU XOR/finite interpolation arguments use learned coefficients; hard-threshold/sigmoid band XOR can use fixed +/− signs. Do not generalize a ReLU limitation to sigmoid or a sigmoid success to ReLU.
- `main.tex:429–439`: exact real-arithmetic nesting holds when all biases equal b and `sum s_k=1`. Odd alternating K satisfies it. Any learned-coefficient K permits `(1,0,...,0)`.
- `multibias/activation.py:106–116`: even-K default instead uses all-positive coefficients and averaging. This remains monotone for monotone bases; it is not a fixed alternating band unit. Identically initialized identical branches under identical deterministic updates can remain identical, explaining the even-K trap already reproduced in the compression study.
- `activation.py:207–224` already proposes a default bias LR multiplier 10 and reports the importance of weight decay; `optim.py:127–150` contains dedicated parameter groups. Thus the user's learning-rate idea is already partly implemented; its optimal value is empirical, not a theorem.
- `multibias/_parametrize.py:28–46` has sorted biases through cumulative softplus; it enforces positive gaps, not a calibrated minimum based on useful gradient magnitude. Its right inverse clamps gaps at 1e−8, so requesting tied biases through sorted mode does not preserve exact ties.
- `multibias/progressive.py:3–13` and `:40–57` already provide progressive K via zero-output new terms. The word “monotonically non-harmful” is justified for the immediate growth operation, not subsequent training/test risk. It also replaces parameter objects and tells callers to rebuild the optimizer; preserving optimizer history needs an explicit migration strategy.
- `multibias/layers.py:196–198`: CNN implementation applies one convolution then the multi-bias activation. It does not compute two Gaussian spatial convolutions.
- `paper/main.tex:815–847` already reports MNIST/CIFAR10 BNN studies, including a depth-one vs depth-four cell. These are repository-reported prior results, not a new verified replication. The new digits compression result is 64 input projections → 16 shared directions, with 64 sigmoid shifts retained and the same one-hidden-layer depth (`omnibias/docs/activation-profile-compression.md:61–83`). It is primarily width/projection compression.

#### 2. Exact nesting gives a useful but limited guarantee

If `H_1` is included in `H_K`, then for the same data, loss, and unconstrained objective:

    inf_{f in H_K} empirical_loss(f) <= inf_{f in H_1} empirical_loss(f).

This concerns the best achievable objective value. It does not imply SGD finds it, a different regularizer preserves the comparison, or held-out accuracy cannot decrease. More parameters can fit noise. A defensible engineering guarantee is to retain the original model as a validation candidate; expanding the candidate set cannot worsen the selected validation score (it still cannot guarantee unseen accuracy).

Exact nesting requires a compatible family. An even alternating sigmoid profile has limit 0 at +infinity, whereas a single sigmoid has limit 1; no finite set of biases gives global equality. Recover the standard unit using odd alternating K, learned coefficients including zero, or an explicit base branch. Strict minimum gaps can exclude tied-bias embeddings unless a base branch or zero coefficients remain available.

Recommended research parameterization:

    phi(z) = sigma(z+b0) + sum_r a_r [sigma(beta(z-t_r+delta_r/2))
                                     - sigma(beta(z-t_r-delta_r/2))].

Initialize `a_r=0`, choose nonzero widths and centers from training projection quantiles, and retain the original branch. This preserves the function while offering an initial gradient into `a_r`; center/width gradients are initially zero until `a_r` moves. Alternatively, add a canceling pair with nonzero opposite coefficients at the same center: function is preserved and independent center gradients are opposite and nonzero wherever the base derivative is nonzero. These are distinct initialization experiments.

An algebraic identity is exact over the reals, but arbitrary floating reduction orders/coefficient representations are not automatically bit-identical. The local identity tests allow error ≤1e−12 (`tests/test_identity_nesting.py:71–76`). The shared-input gradient is preserved by an identity; the newly enlarged parameter gradient vector differs. Pulling it back to the tied-bias submanifold recovers the original parameter gradient.

#### 3. Minimum gap is only half the gradient problem

For a sigmoid band

    B(z) = sigma(beta(z-a)) - sigma(beta(z-b)), a < b,
    delta = b-a,

its maximum occurs at m=(a+b)/2 and exactly equals

    B(m) = tanh(beta*delta/4).

Therefore an intended peak at least tau requires

    delta >= (4/beta) artanh(tau).

This is a useful amplitude criterion. At the same midpoint:

    dB/dz = 0,
    |dB/da| = |dB/db| = beta / [4 cosh^2(beta*delta/4)].

The independent boundary gradients are nonzero for finite beta and delta, while the shared-input/weight gradient cancels. Increasing gap increases peak amplitude but eventually suppresses both boundary gradients at the middle. A minimum gap alone cannot guarantee useful gradients, and tails remain saturated.

A stronger training diagnostic is coverage:

    for every relevant training projection z, some center t_j obeys
    |beta(z-t_j)| <= R and |c_j| >= c_min.

Then that individual threshold parameter has local derivative magnitude at least

    beta*c_min / [4 cosh^2(R/2)].

This is a per-example activation derivative guarantee, not a loss-gradient lower bound: the upstream loss derivative may vanish and batch contributions may cancel. It motivates measuring nearest-center coverage, coefficient size, cancellation, and bias/weight gradient norms separately. It also motivates both minimum and maximum gaps over the high-density projection range, rather than a lower gap bound everywhere.

The common slope and weight normalization matter. Raw gaps or a fixed bias/weight LR ratio do not have a coordinate-invariant meaning when preactivation scales differ between channels. Normalize or track preactivation scale, initialize quantiles in those normalized coordinates, and compare LR multipliers (e.g.1,2,5,10) with equal validation budgets. No theorem selects 10x.

#### 4. 1-D universality: coefficients and slope assumptions matter

For ReLU with learned real coefficients, any continuous function on a compact interval can be approximated by a piecewise-linear spline, represented by an affine term plus shifted hinges. A left-of-domain hinge can supply the affine slope on that bounded domain. This is standard spline algebra and does support 1-D universality as K grows.

For sigmoid, fixed common beta>0 plus unrestricted real output coefficients and biases is also dense on every compact real interval, even without individually learned slopes. A short proof: set t=exp(beta*z), so each translate is h_a(t)=t/(t+a), a>0. On a compact positive t interval, constants are uniform limits as a→0. For a≠b,

    h_a h_b = -a/(b-a) h_a + b/(b-a) h_b.

Squares follow by taking b→a; hence the closed linear span is an algebra containing constants and separating points. Stone–Weierstrass proves density. This existence proof allows large/canceling coefficients and is not a conditioning/efficient-training guarantee. With sum|c_j|≤A every such profile is beta*A/4-Lipschitz, so a fixed coefficient budget limits approximation of steep targets.

The valid-output fixed alternating family is more restricted. With ordered centers, alternating +/- signs beginning positive makes the hard profile a {0,1}-valued union of intervals (possibly a final half-line). Its sigmoid smoothing is convolution with the logistic density k_beta. For any such hard h in [0,1],

    F = h * k_beta,
    |F'| <= (1/2) ||k_beta'||_1 = beta/4.

Thus arbitrary K with a fixed beta does NOT make this family universal for all continuous [0,1]-valued functions: every uniform limit remains beta/4-Lipschitz. For example a unit-height ramp over width epsilon<4/beta requires uniform error at least (1-beta*epsilon/4)/2. The hard Boolean completeness claim permits sharpening/weight scaling and is a different statement.

#### 5. A concrete depth tradeoff (and limit)

Any learned-coefficient sigmoid profile with K common-slope shifts has at most K crossings of any horizontal threshold, unless it equals that threshold identically. After t=exp(beta*z), combine its terms over the positive denominator product_j(t+a_j); the numerator of `F-tau` is a polynomial of degree at most K. Distinct positive roots bound the crossings.

Consequently, if a 1-D target alternates 0/1 at M ordered points, approximation error <1/2 there requires K≥M−1. A deep composition of tent maps has exponentially many alternating values in its depth, so this profile needs exponentially many terms for that family. Richer activations can replace selected depth, including a compact XOR subcircuit; they cannot make arbitrary composition cheap. This is compatible with known depth-separation results, e.g. Telgarsky (2016): https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.04485 .

For multi-dimensional continuous data a single shared projection is constant along its orthogonal hyperplanes, irrespective of K. The conditional-variance floor already derived in the study is the correct obstruction. Boolean finite-set injectivity removes this obstruction only by encoding a finite set in a scalar, possibly at very small margin/high precision.

#### 6. CNN amplitude bands are not spatial DoG

A multi-bias convolutional unit computes

    y(p) = sum_j c_j sigma((K*x)(p)+b_j).

This selects ranges of a filter's response amplitude. DoG computes

    y = (G_s1-G_s2)*x,

which is a linear spatial convolution selecting spatial frequency/scale. The official scikit-image documentation explicitly describes two Gaussian blurs followed by subtraction: https://scikit-image.org/docs/stable/api/skimage.filters.html#skimage.filters.difference_of_gaussians . A DoG can itself be represented by one unconstrained convolution kernel; it is not intrinsically more expressive than a learned arbitrary kernel. The profile is a nonlinear extension after a filter and may be useful for texture/contrast/response-level selectivity. Calling it an amplitude band is accurate; claiming mathematical identity to DoG is generally false. A direct discriminating test is linearity: DoG obeys D(2x)=2D(x), a nontrivial sigmoid-band activation generally does not.

#### 7. Research proposals grounded in these facts

1. An anchored base plus residual profile gives a clean nesting control. Test from scratch and warm-start separately; their costs and learning questions differ.
2. Choose centers by training-only projection quantiles and scale; log coverage and cancellation. Unconstrained minimum gaps and larger LRs are ablations, not universal fixes.
3. Apply dropout to entire residual bands or canceling pairs, preserving the baseline branch. Independent dropout on +/- terms destroys intended cancellation and introduces an unrelated stochastic function.
4. Regularize profile variation/coefficient norm, channel scale, and deviation from the anchored baseline. Large weights alone do not prove overfitting; inspect train/validation gaps and perturbation stability.
5. Vary K by measured per-layer residual/validation gain per added inference byte, rather than assuming K must halve at each depth. Standard CNNs often increase channel width with depth, so “width always halves” is not a universal architecture rule.
6. Keep distinct output coefficients when bands represent different classes. Independent per-band multiclass vectors increase output rank/storage; scalar profiles constrain it. Multiple bands along one projection can represent distinct regions/classes, but they cannot distinguish points sharing that projection.
7. A band-priority/hierarchical rule is a mixture/gating or decision-list model. Explicitly define overlap semantics and normalize gates; it is an architectural proposal, not an automatic property of sum-of-bands.
8. For convergence evidence, report optimization budgets, gradient/coverage curves, best-checkpoint location, train/validation losses, calibration and paired error changes. One cannot promise every nonlinear fit has converged globally or neither over/underfits; define and check operational diagnostics and retain unresolved cases.

#### 8. Paper issues found (no edits made)

- `main.tex:460–462` claims the added left hinge gives a full PWL representation on all R, but `appendix.tex:474–493` only proves it on z>c0 (the input range). Globally every finite sum of identically oriented ReLU hinges has zero left-tail slope. Use a compact-domain statement or include an explicit affine term/oppositely oriented hinge.
- `appendix.tex:451–452` uses g(0) as the affine intercept without subtracting hinge contributions at zero. Correct general identity: `g(z)=a0*z+c+sum Delta_k ReLU(z-c_k)` with `c=g(0)-sum Delta_k ReLU(-c_k)`. This does not undermine compact-domain spline universality.
- `appendix.tex:2951–2968` overstates Gaussian branch gradients: g'(0)=h'(0)=0 and tails are arbitrarily small. Independent sigmoid-band boundaries do have useful additional parameter directions, as the exact formulas above show; that separate argument should replace a universal no-vanishing-gradient claim.

Relevant primary comparisons: learned activation splines (Unser2019, https://jmlr.org/papers/v20/18-418.html), adaptive piecewise-linear activations (Agostinelli et al2015, https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6830), and function-preserving expansion (Net2Net2015, https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.05641). The identities above are established mathematics or direct derivations; novelty needs a concrete new theorem/algorithm beyond their combination.

#### 9. Constructive K/temperature rule, independently checked

For L-Lipschitz f on [a,b], extended constantly beyond the endpoints, choose
K≥1, h=(b−a)/K, x_i=a+ih, t_i=(x_i+x_{i−1})/2, and
c_i=f(x_i)−f(x_{i−1}). Then

    P(x)=f(a)+sum_{i=1}^K c_i sigma(beta*(x−t_i))
    ||P−f_extended||_infinity <= L(b−a)/(2K)+2L*log(2)/beta.

The midpoint staircase S takes nearest-grid f values, so its uniform error is
at most Lh/2. Logistic convolution maps each step to a shifted sigmoid and
has E|Z|=2log(2)/beta. Convolution is nonexpansive in the uniform norm, giving
the displayed error. Coefficients obey |c_i|≤Lh and sum|c_i|≤L(b−a).
For requested error epsilon, K≥ceil(L(b−a)/epsilon) and
beta≥4Llog(2)/epsilon suffice. These are conservative sufficient choices,
not necessary optimal counts. A non-midpoint endpoint staircase gives the
looser requested Lh+2Llog(2)/beta bound.

Complete proof and reproducible checks are saved in
`/tmp/profile_approximation_bound.py` and `/tmp/profile_approximation_bound.json`.
Eight float64 fixtures pass independent numerical staircase-convolution checks
(maximum discrepancy 2.23e−16); four epsilon=.1 parameter-budget constructions
have sampled errors .02164, .02101, .02161 and .04329 for linear, quadratic,
sine and absolute-value functions. Six invalid-input cases are rejected.
Numerical grid checks are explicitly empirical; the analytic proof supplies
the global guarantee. The routine can reject an invalid L on grid points but
cannot infer the true global Lipschitz constant from finitely many samples.

The constructive guarantee uses signed real amplitudes and temperature growth.
It is distinct from the fixed-beta density proof with unrestricted coefficient
cancellation and does not imply fixed-sign Boolean bands have the same bound.

## Appendix 054: omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/profile_model_readonly_audit.md

Source: [omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/profile_model_readonly_audit.md](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/profile_model_readonly_audit.md). Original SHA256: `990d2f093dd75f6152628517fdcebcb666f5b6ed1a8188d7339aedc359c61da9`.

This is the complete source note at compilation time. Its original experiment date, protocol, limitations and historical status apply; later corrections in the overview and subsequent audit notes take precedence. Heading levels, line endings, outer document spacing and source-relative Markdown links are normalized here; code and mathematical expressions are preserved.

### Independent read-only audit of the CNN prototype

Audited `/tmp/multibias_learning_research/models.py` and `data.py`, and the relevant calibration call in `training.py`. No implementation files were edited by this reviewer.

#### Findings communicated before training

1. **Calibration used the wrong BatchNorm regime.** Fresh eval-mode BatchNorm uses mean0/variance1, whereas training normalizes random convolution responses by batch statistics. This placed thresholds on a different response scale. The implementation owner fixed calibration to use `F.batch_norm` with training statistics, without mutating running buffers, and restores mode.
2. **Calibration used a biased subset.** The probe set was random then sorted; taking its first256 chose the smallest source indices. Owner replaced this with a separately seeded uniform256 draw from the training set, and records its IDs/hash.
3. **Calibration subsampling could exceed its claimed cap.** Floor division for stride retained up to nearly twice65536 entries. Owner changed this to ceiling division.
4. **Float64 calibration q dtype.** `torch.quantile` requires q to match the input dtype; its default float32 tensor breaks double-input checks. Sent owner the `dtype=flat.dtype` fix recommendation.

#### Contracts and fairness

- The activation called `sigmoid` is exactly `2*sigmoid(2*z)-1=tanh(z)` over the reals. It must be labeled centered/scaled sigmoid (tanh equivalent), including in the K1 comparator. The implementation owner is doing so. Float32 evaluation differs from `torch.tanh` by rounding, observed maximum1.79e−7 in the small fixture.
- Learned profiles start coefficient0=1 and all extra coefficients0. This exactly nests the K1 network with matched weight initialization, including after quantile placement. The extra bias gradients are initially zero; the extra coefficient gradients need not be. This is an intended staged activation mechanism, not a no-vanishing-gradient guarantee.
- `fixed_k3` has fixed +/−/+ at tied zero biases, so it nests K1 as intended. The hardcoded3-term coefficients are valid for registered recipes but the generic constructor should reject unsupported fixed K if it becomes public.
- The regularized recipe combines residual-term dropout, minimum-gap penalty, bias-box penalty and extra-coefficient L1. It is a joint recipe; its result cannot identify which component helped. Dropout masks are shared across examples/spatial points per channel/term. It is not dropout of explicitly paired sigmoid bands.
- Calibration and normalization use training data only. Validation is stratified500/class and disjoint; test data are loaded/hashed but not used in fitting. Augmentation and minibatch order have separate seeds from dropout, which preserves paired order across recipes.
- Export retains all parameters/buffers, including BatchNorm state and coefficient buffers. Shape/dtype/key/nonfinite checks exist. Recipe topology must accompany arrays through the job/manifest; this file alone is not self-describing.
- Same-channel-width fits are meaningful architecture comparisons but are not exact equal-parameter controls; report the stored arrays/parameters. Runtime-capped unfinished fits must stay unresolved rather than be called convergence failures.
- Norms of all bias gradients pooled together can hide inactive extra branches. For the gradient mechanism claim, per-term or base-vs-extra gradient summaries are more diagnostic. Current activation diagnostics also measure signed-gradient cancellation through the actual summed derivative.

#### Independent tiny CPU checks

`/tmp/profile_model_readonly_audit.py` and `.json` verify:
- K1 vs learnedK3 logits exactly equal before and after calibration in a small CNN fixture.
- BatchNorm running buffers and original eval mode are preserved by calibration.
- Extra-bias gradients are zero at zero coefficients, while extra-coefficient gradients are nonzero (27.724 and−1.302 in the fixture).
- Centered sigmoid agrees numerically with tanh within1.8e−7 float32.

Result: PASS. This is a bounded mechanism audit; no datasets, training studies, timing comparisons or GPU jobs were run by this reviewer.

## Appendix 055: omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/profile_tangent_learning.md

Source: [omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/profile_tangent_learning.md](/home/vardan/dev/projects/omnibias_projects/omnibias-lab/reports/multibias_learning_20261020/profile_tangent_learning.md). Original SHA256: `05b7054f6e3598c698e237601734d3ee3c3d1bca487391bb7153ff9d2a4a189e`.

This is the complete source note at compilation time. Its original experiment date, protocol, limitations and historical status apply; later corrections in the overview and subsequent audit notes take precedence. Heading levels, line endings, outer document spacing and source-relative Markdown links are normalized here; code and mathematical expressions are preserved.

### Tied-profile initialization changes the learning rate in function space

This is an initial tangent calculation and a few analytic update fixtures.
It is not a training result or a new optimization method.

Let \(\phi\) be twice continuously differentiable locally, fix scores \(z_i\), and compare

\[
f_i^{\rm single}=\phi(z_i+b),\qquad
f_i^{\rm multi}=\sum_{j=1}^K c_j\phi(z_i+b_j).
\]

Initially let all \(b_j=b\), with fixed \(c_j\in\{-1,1\}\) and
\(\sum_j c_j=1\). Thus the functions agree exactly. In particular,
\((1,-1,1)\) is a three-term instance. Let \(r_i=\partial L/\partial f_i\)
for the same differentiable empirical loss at this common prediction.
Write \(q_i=\phi'(z_i+b)\) and \(S=q^\top r\).

#### Bias Jacobian and initial SGD dynamics

The single-bias Jacobian is \(J_{\rm single}=q\), while

\[
J_{\rm multi}=q\,c^\top,\qquad
J_{\rm multi}J_{\rm multi}^\top
 =\left(\sum_j c_j^2\right)q q^\top
 =KJ_{\rm single}J_{\rm single}^\top .
\]

The bias parameter gradients are \(S\) and \(c_jS\), respectively.
With the same learning rate \(\eta\), their first-order prediction changes are

\[
\Delta f_{\rm single}=-\eta qS+O(\eta^2),\qquad
\Delta f_{\rm multi}=-K\eta qS+O(\eta^2).
\]

The extra identical branches have amplified the initial learning rate without
adding a new bias tangent direction. The bias parameter Gram matrix has rank
one (when \(q\ne0\)), leaving \(K-1\) unidentifiable initial bias directions.

Using multi-bias learning rate \(\eta/K\) matches the baseline's initial
gradient-flow velocity. It does not make finite steps or later iterates equal.
For a smooth activation with a locally bounded third derivative, the
second-order terms are

\[
f_{\rm multi}^{+}
=f-\eta qS+
\frac{\eta^2 S^2}{2K^2}\phi''(z+b)\sum_j c_j^3+O(\eta^3)
=f-\eta qS+
\frac{\eta^2 S^2}{2K^2}\phi''(z+b)+O(\eta^3),
\]

whereas the baseline's second-order term lacks the \(1/K^2\) factor.
After the biases split, the Jacobian columns are no longer signed copies.
If \(S=0\), every bias gradient here is zero; amplification does not create
a nonzero signal from zero.

For arbitrary fixed real coefficients with \(\sum_jc_j=1\), replace \(K\)
by \(\sum_jc_j^2\) in the SGD tangent formula.

#### Shared weights and coefficient learning must be accounted for separately

If \(z_i=w^\top x_i\), the initial shared-weight derivative is

\[
\nabla_w f_i^{\rm multi}
=\sum_j c_j\phi'(z_i+b)x_i
=\phi'(z_i+b)x_i
=\nabla_w f_i^{\rm single}.
\]

Thus the **whole** Jacobian kernel is not multiplied by \(K\):
it is \(K\) times the bias contribution plus the unchanged shared-weight
contribution. Scaling the bias learning rate by \(1/K\), while retaining the
weight learning rate, matches the initial joint gradient-flow velocity under
these assumptions. Scaling every parameter's learning rate by \(1/K\) does
not. None of these statements establishes equivalence after updating.

An important contrasting initialization is trainable
\(c=(1,0,0)\), with \(b_1=b\) and other biases placed at distinct quantiles.
The function again equals the baseline. Its bias-only Jacobian is
\([q,0,0]\), so there is no \(K\)-fold bias-kernel amplification.
The coefficient Jacobian columns are instead
\(\phi(z_i+b_j)\). If coefficients train, they supply additional tangent
directions immediately; the zero-coefficient branches' bias gradients remain
zero at that initial instant. Bias-only and coefficient-learning effects
must not be conflated.

#### Adam: an exact first-step statement, not a general equivalence

For Adam with initially zero moments, bias correction, no regularization or
weight decay, and positive epsilon added outside the square root, the first update is

\[
\Delta b_j=-\eta\frac{c_jS}{|c_jS|+\epsilon}.
\]

For \(c_j=\pm1\), every update is the signed baseline update. Therefore the
first-order prediction change is again exactly \(K\) times the baseline's
change at the same learning rate (assuming the same epsilon). This remains a
first-order statement about the prediction; the finite nonlinear steps differ.
For arbitrary \(c_j\), \(S\ne0\), the amplification ratio is

\[
(|S|+\epsilon)
\sum_j\frac{c_j^2}{|c_jS|+\epsilon}.
\]

It approaches \(\sum_j|c_j|\) when epsilon is negligible on every nonzero
coefficient path. In contrast, SGD uses \(\sum_jc_j^2\).
Later Adam steps have accumulated, potentially different moments; branches
have split; regularization may alter gradients. The simple formula must not
be extended to those cases.

#### Conditioning and conservative controls

At a general profile, the bias Jacobian has entries

\[
J_{ij}=c_j\phi'(z_i+b_j).
\]

Coincident or nearly coincident centers can give highly correlated columns.
Separated centers may add useful directions, but saturation, weak residual
correlations, and zero coefficients can still remove the signal. A minimum
bias gap alone cannot guarantee useful gradients or well-conditioned learning.

A standard local damping option is the ridge-preconditioned Jacobian step
(the usual Gauss–Newton form for squared residual loss)

\[
\Delta b=-\eta(J^\top J+\lambda I)^{-1}J^\top r,\qquad \lambda>0.
\]

Its linearized prediction response is
\(-\eta J(J^\top J+\lambda I)^{-1}J^\top r\). By the singular-value
decomposition, this operator has eigenvalues
\(s^2/(s^2+\lambda)\in[0,1)\); hence its norm is at most one.
This bounds the local response by \(\eta\|r\|_2\), but does not guarantee
the actual nonlinear objective decreases at an unrestricted finite step.
Backtracking against the actual objective remains appropriate. Damping also
depends on parameter scaling and adds computational cost.

For fair experiments, compare the tied fixed-sign initialization with both
the original baseline bias rate and the initially tangent-matched rate
\(\eta/K\), while preserving weight rates and selection budgets. A requested
2–10× increase in every bias rate would multiply this already \(K\)-amplified
initial response; it is a tuning hypothesis, not a general correction.
Coefficient-zero quantile initialization has a different tangent geometry
and needs its own learning-rate controls.

The kernel calculation is standard Jacobian/gradient-flow algebra. Its general
function-space perspective is developed in [Jacot, Gabriel and Hongler,
*Neural Tangent Kernel*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.07572); this small finite
calculation does not require that paper's infinite-width assumptions.
The damping rule is classical Gauss–Newton/Levenberg–Marquardt methodology.
No mathematical novelty or general performance advantage is claimed.

#### Reproducible checks

`/tmp/profile_tangent_learning.py` uses exact rational sigmoid derivatives
for the kernel identity, and small float64 tanh examples for central finite
differences, actual single SGD steps, Adam's initial update, coefficient-zero
nesting, and the damped local response. The checked values and fingerprints
are stored in `/tmp/profile_tangent_learning.json`. No dataset, optimizer loop,
training run, or GPU is used.
